lessons.title: Efficiency, memory and scalability
lessons.invariant: Compare solutions for the same problem and input model.
lessons.complexity: Time and auxiliary space are separate resources.
lessons.takeaway: A faster structure can spend more memory; scale changes which cost matters.

steps.caption: The task is membership lookup
steps.why: The output contract is the same for both implementations.

steps.caption: Scan an unsorted list
steps.why: A sequential scan may inspect every stored item.

steps.caption: Build an index
steps.why: Extra structure can reduce later lookup work, but it must be built and stored.

steps.caption: Scale from 4 to 4000 items
steps.why: Repeated full scans grow with the list length; an index changes that tradeoff.

steps.caption: Choose using the workload
steps.why: A single tiny query may not justify indexing; many queries often do.

check.question: Why might a faster lookup structure use more memory?
options: All fast algorithms copy the input.
check.explanation: An index stores information that can avoid repeated scanning; this is a workload tradeoff, not a universal law.

lessons.python:
items = [12, 5, 9, 3]
query = 9
comparisons = 0
for value in items:
    comparisons += 1
    if value == query:
        break
index = set(items)
assert query in index
sizes = [4, 40, 400, 4000]
queries = 1000
scan_upper_work = [n * queries for n in sizes]
workload = {'size': len(items), 'queries': queries}
print(comparisons, workload, scan_upper_work)

teaching.motivation: A membership test that is instant for four records can become a bottleneck when thousands of queries repeatedly scan a large collection.
teaching.background: Efficiency describes resources used to solve a specified problem. Runtime measures work, memory measures stored information, and scalability asks how those demands change as the input grows. Comparisons are meaningful only when solutions meet the same output contract.
teaching.objective: Compare a repeated scan with an index using input size, query count and memory budget.
applications: Repeated student-ID checks can justify a membership index because one construction serves many queries.
A memory-limited device may prefer scanning a short list because extra indexing storage is costly.
teaching.summary: The four-item lookup becomes a workload decision: scanning avoids setup, while indexing spends storage and construction work to help later queries. Input size alone does not determine the best choice.
teaching.next: Runtime analysis supplies a language for predicting these costs; ADTs explain which behavior competing implementations must preserve.
bridges: We need to determine whether 9 occurs in [12,5,9,3]. The diagram fixes the data and desired answer before the code chooses a representation.
The scan now checks 12, then 5, then 9; the highlighted prefix explains why the counter reaches three. Stopping at the match avoids inspecting 3.
Instead of repeating that scan, the code constructs a set containing the same values. Its construction and storage are additional costs paid to support later membership checks.
Now imagine keeping the same scan policy while growing the collection to 4000 records. The displayed work sizes make the cost of repeating a full scan visible.
The final diagram brings size, query count and memory together. Use those workload facts to decide whether the index saves enough repeated work to justify its setup.

lessons.title: Data structures and algorithms in everyday tasks
lessons.invariant: A structure organizes data; an algorithm is a procedure that uses it.
lessons.complexity: Cost depends on both representation and procedure.
lessons.takeaway: Identify the stored relationships before choosing the steps.

steps.caption: A dictionary stores ordered entries
steps.why: Organized entries allow a lookup procedure to narrow its search.

steps.caption: A folder index stores locations
steps.why: The index maps a name to a place rather than being the search procedure itself.

steps.caption: Routes store connected places
steps.why: A map representation records which locations are connected.

steps.caption: Navigation chooses steps
steps.why: A route-finding procedure explores those relationships according to its objective.

steps.caption: Menus organize available choices
steps.why: Selecting an option is a procedure over the organized choices.

check.question: Which is an algorithm?
options: A procedure that explores roads to find a route
check.explanation: The procedure specifies steps; the table and folder are representations.

lessons.python:
entries = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
assert entries.index('B') == 1
folder_index = {'notes.txt': '/course/notes.txt'}
location = folder_index['notes.txt']
graph = {'home': ['junction'], 'junction': ['campus'], 'campus': []}
neighbors = graph['home']
route = ['home']
route.append(neighbors[0])
route.append(graph[route[-1]][0])
menu = {'search': 'membership lookup', 'insert': 'add item', 'delete': 'remove item'}
choice = 'search'
print(location, route, menu[choice])

teaching.motivation: Before choosing a search or navigation algorithm, we need to know what the stored data represents and what question the procedure must answer.
teaching.background: A data structure organizes values and relationships; an algorithm specifies steps over that organization. The same distinction appears in dictionaries, file indexes, road maps and menus, even though the stored items and desired outputs differ.
teaching.objective: Distinguish a stored representation from the procedure operating on it in familiar applications.
applications: A document index maps filenames to locations so an opening procedure can retrieve the selected file.
A navigation service stores road connections, then uses a route procedure to choose a path.
teaching.summary: Entries, mappings and connections are stored descriptions. Looking up a word, following a route and dispatching a menu choice are procedures that use those descriptions.
teaching.next: ADTs turn these application expectations into explicit contracts; later search and graph lessons provide concrete procedures.
bridges: Begin with entries A through D and a request for B. The boxes are the organized data; the highlighted lookup in the code is the action performed on them.
The example switches to a filename-to-location mapping. Retrieving notes.txt illustrates how an index stores enough information for a procedure to find the document.
For navigation, the data changes from a mapping of names to locations into connected places. The diagram shows home, junction and campus as relationships to explore.
Starting at home, the code follows the stored neighbor relationships to reach campus. That sequence of actions is distinct from the graph that makes those actions possible.
The menu example makes the distinction once more: the available choices are stored, and selecting search dispatches the corresponding behavior.

lessons.title: Abstract data types and information hiding
lessons.invariant: The public operation contract does not expose its internal representation.
lessons.complexity: Two implementations can satisfy one ADT with different operation costs.
lessons.takeaway: Ask what an operation promises before asking how it works.

steps.caption: Specify the list contract
steps.why: An ordered collection can promise access, insertion and removal without naming a representation.

steps.caption: Observe the logical sequence
steps.why: A client sees values in their documented order.

steps.caption: Choose an array representation
steps.why: Contiguous slots can implement the same logical order.

steps.caption: Choose a linked representation
steps.why: A chain of nodes can preserve the same order through links.

steps.caption: Keep clients independent
steps.why: Changing internals should preserve the contract even when operation costs change.

check.question: What does information hiding protect?
options: Clients from depending on internal representation
The program from all runtime errors
check.explanation: The ADT specifies observable behavior, allowing internal representation and algorithms to change.

teaching.motivation: A program should be able to use a list without depending on whether its values live in an array or in linked nodes.
teaching.background: An abstract data type, or ADT, defines legal values and operations by their observable behavior. An implementation supplies storage and algorithms. Information hiding keeps clients dependent on the contract rather than on internal fields or pointer arrangements.
teaching.objective: Explain how two different representations can satisfy the same list-access contract.
applications: A library can replace its internal storage while preserving documented get and insert behavior.
Testing an ADT contract checks results and order across implementations without inspecting private fields.
teaching.summary: Both representations return 4 at position 1 in [7,4,9]. Their access procedures differ, but a client using only get observes the same logical result.
teaching.next: Arrays and linked lists show how that shared contract leads to different indexing, insertion and deletion costs.
bridges: The public operations define what a list user may request. In the Python listing, both sequence classes expose get rather than requiring the caller to manipulate storage.
Fix the logical sequence [7,4,9] and request position 1. The expected value 4 belongs to the contract, regardless of representation.
The array version reads storage[1] directly. Its boxes preserve the same logical order using contiguous indexed positions.
The linked version starts at head and follows a link before reading the value. The different route to 4 demonstrates why behavior and mechanism are separate.
The final assertion calls get on both objects without checking their type. Equal values, order and interface are what make implementation replacement possible.

lessons.title: Python runtime, dynamic types and managed memory
lessons.source: Slide 1 p8; 01-lang-intro cells 3-18,43-48. Clarifies the slide shorthand about interpreted execution.
lessons.invariant: Names refer to objects; each object has its own type.
lessons.complexity: Costs depend on executed operations; Python integers are arbitrary precision.
lessons.takeaway: Rebinding changes a reference; it does not change the old object into a new type.

steps.caption: Bind a name to an integer
steps.why: Dynamic typing means objects have runtime types and a name can later refer to another type.

steps.caption: Rebind the same name
steps.why: The integer is not converted in place; x now refers to a string object.

steps.caption: Execute a Python function
steps.why: CPython typically compiles source to bytecode and executes it in an interpreter.

steps.caption: Share an object with another name
steps.why: Automatic memory management tracks object reachability; names need not own separate copies.

steps.caption: Remove a reference
steps.why: Deleting a name removes that binding; an object can remain alive through other references.

check.question: After x = 7; x = "seven", what happened?
options: The int object changed its type
x was rebound to a string object
check.explanation: Object types still matter at runtime. A name can be rebound to an object of a different type.

lessons.python:
x = 7
assert type(x) is int
x = 'seven'
assert type(x) is str
def increment(value):
    return value + 1
result = increment(3)
a = [1, 2]
b = a
del a
assert b == [1, 2]
print(result, b)

teaching.motivation: Many list bugs begin when a programmer treats assignment as copying an object or assumes that a variable permanently has one type.
teaching.background: Python names refer to objects, and objects have runtime types. Assignment can rebind a name to another object. In CPython, source is normally compiled to bytecode for interpretation, while automatic memory management tracks references and reclaims unreachable objects.
teaching.objective: Trace rebinding and shared references without confusing a name with the object it refers to.
applications: Understanding shared references prevents accidental changes to data passed into a function.
Knowing object lifetime helps explain why deleting one variable does not necessarily release its list.
teaching.summary: Rebinding x changed which object x referred to; it did not transform an integer into a string. Sharing a list gave two names access to one object, which remained reachable after one name was deleted.
teaching.next: Identity, equality and mutable-list aliasing make these reference relationships observable in code.
bridges: Bind x to the integer 7. The diagram represents a reference from a name to an object, and type(x) confirms the object type at runtime.
The assignment replaces that binding with the string seven. The new object has type str; the previous integer was not modified into text.
Calling increment adds an execution layer to the object model. The diagram names source, bytecode and runtime rather than claiming that Python never compiles anything.
Now a and b are bound to the same list. The two labels in the diagram describe shared access, not two independently copied lists.
Deleting a removes one binding while b still reaches the list. The surviving reference explains why the code can continue to read its contents.

lessons.title: Indentation, branching and loops
lessons.invariant: The current block determines which statement executes next.
lessons.complexity: A loop cost is its iteration count times the work per iteration.
lessons.takeaway: Indentation is syntax; a for loop, while loop and break change control flow.

steps.caption: Start outside the block
steps.why: Whitespace defines a suite of statements after a colon.

steps.caption: First iteration fails the condition
steps.why: The assignment inside the if block is skipped for x=1.

steps.caption: Second iteration enters the block
steps.why: x=2 satisfies the condition, so the nested update runs.

steps.caption: Third iteration updates again
steps.why: The loop visits each element once; total is now 5.

steps.caption: A while loop tests again; break exits
steps.why: Use a progress measure to ensure a while loop terminates; break leaves the innermost loop.

check.question: What determines whether total += x belongs to the if block?
check.explanation: Python uses indentation to define suites under if, for, while and function definitions.

teaching.motivation: Reading an algorithm correctly requires knowing which updates run on each iteration and which are skipped by a condition.
teaching.background: Python uses indentation to define statement blocks after constructs such as if, for and while. A for loop visits an iterable; a while loop repeats while a condition is true. break exits the nearest enclosing loop, so its position changes the execution path.
teaching.objective: Trace nested blocks and explain when a loop update or break executes.
applications: A filter counts only records satisfying its condition because the update is inside the if block.
A search loop can stop as soon as it finds a match by executing break.
teaching.summary: The total changed only for 2 and 3 because the update belonged to the conditional block. The countdown then demonstrated that a while test and an explicit break control repetition differently.
teaching.next: Operation counting and loop invariants build on this ability to trace exactly which statements execute.
bridges: Set total to zero before entering the for block. The highlighted code makes the nesting explicit: only the most deeply indented update depends on x > 1.
At x=1, the condition is false, so the update is skipped and total stays zero. A loop iteration need not execute every statement written in its body.
At x=2, the condition becomes true and the nested update adds two. Connect the highlighted input cell to the new accumulator value.
The next iteration adds three to the existing two, producing five. The diagram records the cumulative effect rather than resetting total each time.
The countdown uses a while condition and decreases n to make progress. When n reaches zero, break leaves that loop immediately; indentation determines which loop owns it.

lessons.title: Numbers, conversion and truth values
lessons.invariant: Evaluate an expression using operand types and the operator semantics.
lessons.complexity: Treat bounded-size arithmetic as O(1) only when that model is appropriate.
lessons.takeaway: Division, floor division, remainder and truth conversion answer different questions.

steps.caption: Start with integer operands
steps.why: The operands here are integers.

steps.caption: Regular division produces a float
steps.why: The / operator gives a floating-point quotient for these operands.

steps.caption: Floor division and remainder partition
steps.why: For positive b, a = (a//b)*b + a%b; floor division rounds toward negative infinity.

steps.caption: Convert values explicitly
steps.why: Conversions may fail when the representation is invalid; str formats a value rather than mutating it.

steps.caption: Use truth values in conditions
steps.why: Zero and empty containers are false; nonzero numbers and nonempty containers are true.

check.question: What is 7 // 3 and 7 % 3?
check.explanation: Floor division gives 2 and remainder gives 1, satisfying 7 = 2*3+1.

lessons.python:
a, b = 7, 3
quotient = a / b
assert isinstance(quotient, float)
q, r = a // b, a % b
assert a == q * b + r
n = int('12')
s = str(n)
truth_values = [bool(v) for v in [0, [], 3, [0]]]
assert truth_values == [False, False, True, True]
print(quotient, q, r, s, truth_values)

teaching.motivation: Remainders, integer indices and empty-container checks appear throughout data-structure algorithms, so their Python meanings must be precise.
teaching.background: Python distinguishes integer and floating-point arithmetic, division and floor division, and explicit value conversion. Conditions apply truth conversion: numeric zero and empty containers are false. For positive divisors, quotient and remainder reconstruct the original integer.
teaching.objective: Predict arithmetic, conversion and truth-test results used in algorithm code.
applications: Floor division computes a midpoint index without producing a floating-point array index.
A nonempty-stack condition prevents accessing the top of an empty stack.
teaching.summary: The operations on 7 and 3 answered different questions: / produced a fractional quotient, while // and % gave quotient and remainder. Conversions and truth checks then translated values into forms needed by later code.
teaching.next: Binary-search indices, hash formulas and guarded stack operations rely on these rules.
bridges: Start with integer operands 7 and 3. Their types and the selected operator together determine what the expression produces.
The / operator returns a float for these operands, so the quotient is approximately 2.333 rather than the integer 2.
Switching to // and % produces 2 and 1. The code checks 7 = 2*3+1, which explains the relationship between the two results.
The conversion example changes the representation explicitly, from text 12 to integer 12 and back. Conversion creates a usable value; it does not edit the original text object.
Finally, the diagram compares false zero/empty values with true nonzero/nonempty values. Notice that [0] is true because the container is nonempty even though its element is zero.

lessons.title: Strings, ranges, tuples and slicing
lessons.invariant: A slice includes start and excludes stop; negative indices count from the end.
lessons.complexity: Sequence indexing is O(1) for built-in str/tuple/range; a copied slice costs O(k).
lessons.takeaway: Immutability prevents item replacement; it does not mean a name cannot be rebound.

steps.caption: Index a sequence from zero
steps.why: The index is a position, not the stored value.

steps.caption: Count backward from the end
steps.why: Index -1 refers to the final element.

steps.caption: Take a half-open slice
steps.why: s[1:4] includes indices 1,2,3 and excludes 4.

steps.caption: Use a stepped range
steps.why: range stores bounds and step rather than materializing all values.

steps.caption: Understand immutable containers
steps.why: Tuple slots cannot be replaced; an object stored in a tuple can itself be mutable.

check.question: Which positions does s[1:4] select?
check.explanation: Python uses half-open slice bounds: start is included, stop is excluded.

lessons.python:
s = 'CS331'
assert s[0] == 'C'
assert s[-1] == '1'
assert s[1:4] == 'S33'
assert list(range(1, 7, 2)) == [1, 3, 5]
t = (7, [1])
t[1].append(2)
assert t == (7, [1, 2])
print(s, t)

teaching.motivation: Indexing and slicing look similar, but an off-by-one interpretation can select the wrong data or hide the cost of copying it.
teaching.background: A sequence preserves positional order. Python indices start at zero, negative indices count from the end, and slices include start but exclude stop. Strings and tuples cannot have their slots replaced; range represents an arithmetic progression without storing every generated value.
teaching.objective: Read indices and slice boundaries and distinguish immutable slots from mutable referenced objects.
applications: A text parser uses half-open slices to extract exactly the intended characters.
A range supplies loop positions lazily without allocating a list of every index.
teaching.summary: The CS331 example connected forward indexing, backward indexing and a half-open slice. Range then separated a generated sequence from stored values, while the tuple example showed that immutable slots can still reference mutable objects.
teaching.next: Array access and binary search require these positional conventions; aliasing explains the nested tuple example.
bridges: The string CS331 has positions 0 through 4. The first highlighted character shows why s[0] returns C rather than the second character.
Using -1 selects the final position from the opposite direction. The underlying sequence has not been reversed or copied.
The slice s[1:4] highlights S,3,3 and leaves position 4 out. The displayed S33 result follows directly from the excluded stop bound.
The range example emits 1,3,5 using step two and stops before seven. Its bounds describe the sequence without requiring all values to be stored.
The tuple holds an integer and a list reference. Appending through that reference changes the list while the tuple keeps the same two slots.

lessons.title: Mutable lists, aliasing and copies
lessons.invariant: Aliased names observe the same mutations; a shallow copy has distinct outer storage.
lessons.complexity: List indexing O(1); copying O(n); append amortized O(1); sorting O(n log n) worst case.
lessons.takeaway: Assignment shares references; copying and sorting have explicit semantics.

steps.caption: Create a list and an alias
steps.why: b=a copies a reference, not the list elements.

steps.caption: Mutate through the alias
steps.why: Replacing b[0] is visible through a because both names reference the same list.

steps.caption: Make a shallow outer copy
steps.why: c=a[:] creates another outer list; nested objects would still be shared.

steps.caption: Sort into a new list
steps.why: sorted(a) leaves a unchanged, while a.sort() mutates and returns None.

steps.caption: Convert between text and words
steps.why: split creates words from text; join combines strings with a separator.

check.question: After b=a and b.append(4), does a contain 4?
options: Yes, a and b share the list.
Only if the list was empty.
check.explanation: Both names refer to the same mutable list object.

lessons.python:
a = [3, 1, 2]
b = a
b[0] = 9
assert a[0] == 9
c = a[:]
assert c is not a
d = sorted(a)
assert d == [1, 2, 9] and a == [9, 1, 2]
words = 'CS 331'.split()
joined = ' '.join(words)
assert joined == 'CS 331'
print(a, c, d, words)

teaching.motivation: If two variables refer to one list, an update through either name can unexpectedly change what the other part of the program sees.
teaching.background: A list is a mutable ordered container. Assignment shares its object reference, while a shallow copy creates new outer storage but shares any referenced nested objects. sorted returns a new list; list.sort modifies its receiver and returns None.
teaching.objective: Predict the effects of assignment, mutation, copying and sorting on related lists.
applications: Copying outer list storage lets a function reorder its own list without reordering the caller original.
Text processing uses split to create words and join to assemble strings with a chosen separator.
teaching.summary: The alias observed the same replacement as the original name, while a slice created separate outer storage. Sorting and text conversion then illustrated operations that create new results rather than silently preserving all identities.
teaching.next: Identity tests and reference diagrams make aliasing precise; dynamic arrays explain how list storage grows.
bridges: Create [3,1,2] and bind both a and b to it. The diagram is one shared list, so assignment alone has not duplicated any element storage.
Writing b[0]=9 changes that shared object. Reading a[0] now returns nine because a and b still reach the same list.
The slice assigned to c creates a different outer list with the same current elements. For nested objects, this would still be only a shallow separation.
sorted(a) produces [1,2,9] while a remains [9,1,2]. Connect the new ordered boxes to the returned value, rather than assuming the original list was rearranged.
The final example creates words with split, then combines them with a space using join. Both transformations make explicit how text and lists of strings relate.

lessons.title: Mappings, sets and hashable keys
lessons.invariant: Dictionary keys are unique; a set stores unique elements.
lessons.complexity: Expected dictionary/set lookup O(1) under suitable hashing; worst O(n).
lessons.takeaway: A mapping answers key-to-value questions; a set answers membership questions.

steps.caption: Create a mapping
steps.why: Keys identify values; they are not integer positions unless chosen that way.

steps.caption: Update an existing key
steps.why: Assigning to a key replaces its value rather than adding a duplicate key.

steps.caption: Handle missing keys deliberately
steps.why: get can return a default without inserting; setdefault can insert a missing key.

steps.caption: Remove duplicates with a set
steps.why: Repeated equal elements are represented once. Iteration order is not a sorted order.

steps.caption: Combine sets and iterate mappings
steps.why: Intersection retains shared members. Hashable keys must have stable hashes while stored.
steps.code:
s & {2, 3, 4}
for key, value in d.items(): ...

check.question: What happens when d["a"] is assigned twice?
options: The existing key gets a new value.
check.explanation: A dictionary stores one entry per key; assignment updates the associated value.

teaching.motivation: A list position is not always the natural way to identify information; applications often need a value by name or need to know whether an item occurs at all.
teaching.background: A dictionary maps unique hashable keys to values. A set stores unique hashable members without a sorted-order contract. Hashability requires a stable hash and consistent equality while an object is stored; expected lookup speed depends on suitable hashing.
teaching.objective: Choose mapping or membership operations and predict updates, defaults and duplicate removal.
applications: A configuration dictionary retrieves a setting by its name instead of scanning positional records.
A set of seen identifiers removes duplicates and supports repeated membership checks.
teaching.summary: Updating a key replaced its value, and a default handled a previously missing key. The set example removed duplicate 2s, then intersection retained only members shared with another set.
teaching.next: Hash tables explain how these interfaces can provide fast expected lookup and what happens when keys collide.
bridges: The initial mapping associates a with 2 and b with 5. The code retrieves by key, not by a numeric list position.
Assigning d["a"]=7 updates the existing entry, so the mapping still has two keys. The changed cell represents replacement, not a duplicate a.
setdefault inserts c only because c is missing. The accompanying get example shows that requesting a fallback can avoid insertion when that is the desired behavior.
Constructing a set from [1,2,2,3] merges the equal 2 values into one member. The diagram does not promise that later set iteration is sorted.
Intersection keeps 2 and 3 because they occur in both sets. Iterating d.items separately demonstrates that a mapping provides key-value pairs, not only values.

lessons.title: Comprehensions and nested iteration
lessons.invariant: Each emitted value corresponds to an iteration combination that passes the filter.
lessons.complexity: A comprehension has the same iteration cost as its equivalent loops.
lessons.takeaway: Compact syntax does not remove nested work.

steps.caption: Start with an input sequence
steps.why: The comprehension evaluates the expression for each selected element.
steps.code: [x*x for x in values if x % 2 == 0]

steps.caption: Reject an odd value
steps.why: A filter skips the output expression when its condition is false.

steps.caption: Emit the square of 2
steps.why: The output contains transformed values, not the original selected values.

steps.caption: Skip 3 and emit 16
steps.why: The order of emitted values follows iteration order.

steps.caption: Nested clauses multiply combinations
steps.why: Two two-element loops generate four pairs; filters may reduce output but still inspect combinations.
steps.code: [(x,y) for x in [1,2] for y in ["a","b"]]

check.question: Does replacing nested loops with a comprehension automatically improve Big-O?
options: No, the same combinations are still visited.
check.explanation: Comprehensions change expression syntax, not the underlying number of iterations.

lessons.python:
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
output = []
for x in values:
    if x % 2 == 0:
        output.append(x*x)
assert output == [x*x for x in values if x % 2 == 0]
pairs = [(x,y) for x in [1,2] for y in ['a','b']]
assert len(pairs) == 4
print(output, pairs)

teaching.motivation: Compact Python can hide a large number of iterations; understanding a comprehension as loops prevents both logic errors and mistaken complexity claims.
teaching.background: A comprehension builds output by iterating, optionally filtering, and evaluating an output expression. Multiple for clauses are nested in written order. A filter can reduce the number of results without reducing all candidate checks that precede it.
teaching.objective: Expand a comprehension into equivalent loops and distinguish candidates from emitted output.
applications: A data-cleaning comprehension selects valid measurements and transforms only those into output.
Generating all candidate pairs for a search still performs nested work even when the final result is small.
teaching.summary: The filter selected even inputs, and the expression squared them to produce 4 and 16. The pair example then showed that compact syntax still generates all four loop combinations.
teaching.next: Pythagorean-triple enumeration extends the same idea to three nested loops and an equality filter.
bridges: Start with [1,2,3,4] and an empty output list. The comprehension has two separate jobs: test parity and square values that pass.
For x=1, the parity condition is false. The highlighted input therefore contributes no output value.
For x=2, the condition succeeds and the output expression produces four. The diagram shows a transformed value rather than simply copying two.
Three is skipped and four contributes sixteen, completing [4,16]. The equivalent loop and comprehension assertions confirm the same selection and order.
Adding another for clause creates combinations: each number is paired with both letters. The four boxes expose work that a short expression can otherwise conceal.

lessons.title: Functions, arguments and returned values
lessons.invariant: Each call binds parameters to arguments and returns control to its caller.
lessons.complexity: Function-call overhead is separate from the work inside the function.
lessons.takeaway: Return values communicate results; defaults and shared mutable arguments require care.

steps.caption: Define a function
steps.why: A definition creates a function object; its body runs when called.
steps.code:
def add(a, b=2):
    return a + b

steps.caption: Bind a positional argument
steps.why: An omitted optional argument uses its default.

steps.caption: Return a computed value
steps.why: The caller receives 5 and the call frame finishes.

steps.caption: Override by keyword
steps.why: Keyword arguments name parameters explicitly.

steps.caption: Pass functions and avoid mutable defaults
steps.why: Functions are values. A mutable default is created once, so use None when each call needs fresh storage.

check.question: When is a default argument expression evaluated?
check.explanation: A default object is created at definition time, which is why mutable defaults can share state across calls.

lessons.python:
def add(a, b=2):
    return a + b
result = add(3)
assert result == 5
assert add(3, b=7) == 10
def collect(x, out=None):
    if out is None:
        out = []
    out.append(x)
    return out
function_value = add
assert function_value(1) == 3
assert collect(1) == [1] and collect(2) == [2]
print(result)

teaching.motivation: Algorithms become easier to reuse when inputs, local work and returned results have a clear boundary.
teaching.background: A function definition creates a callable object. Calling it binds arguments to parameters, executes a new local frame and returns a value to the caller. Defaults are evaluated at definition time; mutable default objects can therefore be shared across calls unless handled deliberately.
teaching.objective: Trace positional and keyword argument binding and design a fresh per-call mutable result.
applications: A search function can accept data and target arguments and return its answer without relying on global state.
A collector using a None default avoids accidentally sharing one output list across unrelated calls.
teaching.summary: The same add function used a default for one call and an explicit keyword for another. The collector example then showed why per-call mutable state should be created inside the function rather than stored as a reusable default.
teaching.next: Methods apply these calling rules to objects; recursion adds nested calls that retain unfinished work.
bridges: Define add(a,b=2) without yet executing its body. The diagram names the required parameter, optional parameter and expression that will produce the result.
Calling add(3) binds a to three and uses the existing default two for b. The shown frame explains which values the body receives.
The return expression combines those arguments into five and passes it to result. The function local names are not themselves the returned value.
Calling add(3,b=7) overrides only the optional argument and returns ten. Keyword binding makes that choice explicit.
The collector uses None as a signal to allocate a fresh list inside each call. Passing add as a function value also demonstrates that callable objects can be stored and invoked through another name.

lessons.title: Objects, methods, inheritance and special methods
lessons.invariant: An instance stores its own state; a method receives the instance through self.
lessons.complexity: Class structure defines interfaces; operation costs depend on method implementations.
lessons.takeaway: Use a class to keep state and the operations maintaining it together.

steps.caption: Define a class and initializer
steps.why: __init__ initializes an existing new instance; self names that instance.

steps.caption: Create independent instances
steps.why: Separate objects can hold different instance attributes.

steps.caption: Call a method on one instance
steps.why: a.increment() binds self to a; b remains unchanged.

steps.caption: Connect syntax to special methods
steps.why: len(x), iteration and string representation call protocol methods where defined.

steps.caption: Extend through inheritance
steps.why: A subclass can override behavior and call a base implementation with super(). Class attributes are shared unless shadowed.

check.question: In a.method(), what does self refer to inside the method?
options: The class name as a string
check.explanation: Method binding supplies the object a as the first parameter.

teaching.motivation: A data structure needs both stored state and operations that keep that state valid; classes provide a way to package them together.
teaching.background: A class defines how instances are initialized and what methods they support. self is the instance receiving a method call. Special methods connect objects to Python protocols such as len, iter and repr; inheritance allows a subclass to refine behavior promised by a base class.
teaching.objective: Trace independent instance state, bound method calls and an overridden subclass operation.
applications: A linked-list class keeps head and its update methods together so clients do not rewire links directly.
A shape interface lets callers request area while circle-specific code computes the appropriate formula.
teaching.summary: The two counters retained independent values, and increment changed only its receiver. Protocol methods made those objects work with familiar Python syntax, while Circle supplied a concrete area behavior through inheritance.
teaching.next: Node and container classes use these mechanisms to represent arrays, linked lists, stacks and trees.
bridges: The Counter definition introduces value storage and the operations that can change it. __init__ receives self so initialization applies to a particular new instance.
Creating a at zero and b at five produces separate state. The two diagram cells should not be interpreted as a shared class-wide counter.
a.increment() changes only a.value to one. The unchanged b cell explains how the bound receiver controls which instance is updated.
The protocol names connect explicit methods to len(a), iter(a) and repr(a). The code shows the implementations that make those otherwise generic operations meaningful.
Circle inherits initialization from Shape and overrides area. Calling Circle(2).area uses the subclass formula while preserving the expected area interface.

lessons.title: Object identity, equality and references
lessons.invariant: is compares object identity; == asks the objects to compare values.
lessons.complexity: Identity testing is O(1); equality cost depends on the objects compared.
lessons.takeaway: Use == for values and is None for the singleton sentinel.

steps.caption: Create two equal lists
steps.why: Equal contents do not imply the same object.

steps.caption: Create an alias
steps.why: The new name c points to the same object as a.

steps.caption: Mutate the shared object
steps.why: An identity relationship explains why both names observe this update.

steps.caption: Do not rely on integer caching
steps.why: Implementation interning can reuse immutable objects; value equality should not depend on that.

steps.caption: Test the None sentinel by identity
steps.why: None is a singleton used for missing or absent values.

check.question: Two separately created lists have equal elements. Must a is b be true?
options: No, equality does not imply identity.
Yes, Python merges all equal lists.
check.explanation: Lists can compare equal while occupying distinct objects.

lessons.python:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
assert a == b and a is not b
c = a
assert c is a
c[1] = 9
assert a == [1, 9] and b == [1, 2]
x, y = int('1000'), int('1000')
assert x == y
value = None
assert value is None
print(a, b)

teaching.motivation: A debugging question can ask either whether two values are equal or whether two names reach the very same object; those are different tests.
teaching.background: Equality, written ==, follows the value-comparison behavior of the objects. Identity, written is, tests whether references point to one object. Immutable-object interning can make some identities coincide accidentally; program logic should not depend on those implementation choices.
teaching.objective: Choose == or is deliberately and explain aliasing through object identity.
applications: Value comparisons such as matching a search target should use == even when Python caches some integers.
Testing value is None distinguishes a missing-result sentinel without asking a user object to define equality with it.
teaching.summary: Separate lists began equal but had different identities. An alias shared identity and observed mutation, while None illustrated an appropriate identity test for a documented singleton sentinel.
teaching.next: Linked-list algorithms use identity to detect the same node even when distinct nodes contain equal values.
bridges: Create a and b separately with equal elements [1,2]. The diagram separates the two objects, so == is true while is is false.
Binding c=a adds a reference to the first object. No second list is created, which is exactly what a is c tests.
Updating through c changes the object reached by a but leaves b untouched. Equality now differs as well because the contents are [1,9] and [1,2].
The integer example deliberately compares values with ==. Whether a particular runtime reuses immutable integer objects is not part of the desired value comparison.
The final check uses is None for the missing-value sentinel. This is an identity question because None denotes one singleton object.

lessons.title: Measuring runtime with repeatable experiments
lessons.source: Slide 2 pp1-3; 02-timing cells 3-18. Timing values are illustrative.
lessons.invariant: Keep the measured operation and workload definition consistent across sizes.
lessons.complexity: Observed seconds are evidence about one environment, not an asymptotic proof.
lessons.takeaway: Repeat measurements, separate setup, and report exactly what was timed.

steps.caption: Choose the operation
steps.why: Fix the code and input family before varying n.

steps.caption: Separate setup from the timed statement
steps.why: Repeatedly constructing inputs can otherwise dominate the operation of interest.

steps.caption: Normalize by repetitions
steps.why: timeit reports total time across number executions, not a per-call time.

steps.caption: Repeat and record noise
steps.why: Other processes and caching affect results. These values are illustrative, not measured here.

steps.caption: Combine evidence with analysis
steps.why: Finite observations cannot uniquely determine behavior for arbitrarily large n.

check.question: timeit returns 2 seconds for number=1000. What is the average per call?
check.explanation: Divide the total measurement by the number of executions.

lessons.python:
import timeit
sizes = [100, 200, 400, 800]
number = 1000
totals = [timeit.timeit('sum(r)', setup=f'r=range({n})', number=number) for n in sizes]
per_call = [total / number for total in totals]
samples = timeit.repeat('sum(r)', setup='r=range(100)', number=number, repeat=5)
operation_counts = sizes[:]
assert len(operation_counts) == len(per_call)
print('Actual measurements vary:', per_call, samples)

teaching.motivation: Before replacing working code, we need evidence about how much time its intended operation actually takes under a defined workload.
teaching.background: Empirical analysis runs code and records elapsed time. Input construction, repetitions, caching and other processes can influence measurements. timeit separates setup from a timed statement and reports a total across repeated executions; dividing by the repetition count estimates a per-call time.
teaching.objective: Design a repeatable timing comparison and explain what its results can and cannot establish.
applications: Comparing two membership implementations requires timing equivalent queries rather than including setup in only one measurement.
Repeated measurements help distinguish a consistent slowdown from unrelated operating-system noise.
teaching.summary: The experiment varied size while fixing the operation and separated setup from timing. Normalization and repetition made the measurements interpretable, but finite seconds on one machine still did not prove an asymptotic bound.
teaching.next: Timing plots reveal patterns; operation counts and asymptotic analysis test whether those patterns have an algorithmic explanation.
bridges: We will time sum over ranges of sizes 100,200,400,800. These sizes define an input family; they are not timing observations themselves.
The timeit call constructs r in setup and times sum(r) repeatedly. Separating those lines prevents us from accidentally calling construction cost a summation cost.

The diagram uses illustrative totals to explain normalization: one millisecond across 1000 calls is 0.001 milliseconds per call. The executable listing reports actual measurements, which vary by machine.
Repeated trials produce slightly different totals even for one size. Treat that variation as part of measurement, rather than choosing one noisy result as an exact cost law.
The final comparison brings measurements together with operation counts. A measured trend is useful evidence, but only a stated model explains behavior beyond the tested samples.

lessons.title: Plotting timings and avoiding misleading curve fits
lessons.source: 02-timing cells 19-42; Slide 2 p3. Values are illustrative.
lessons.invariant: Each plotted y value corresponds to the same-position x input size.
lessons.complexity: Fitting a curve to finite samples does not prove the growth class.
lessons.takeaway: Use correct axes, paired data and theory before extrapolating.

steps.caption: Pair size and runtime
steps.why: Equal-length sequences define coordinate pairs.

steps.caption: Read a doubling ratio
steps.why: This illustrative data doubles time when size doubles, consistent with linear growth.

steps.caption: Compare a theoretical model
steps.why: A scaled linear model can fit without implying exact seconds on another machine.

steps.caption: A high-degree polynomial can overfit
steps.why: Matching observed points need not yield useful predictions beyond the sampled interval.

steps.caption: Use sampling tools deliberately
steps.why: linspace chooses a count of evenly spaced points; arange uses a step. Materialize generators when required by the plotting API.

check.question: Does an excellent polynomial fit prove an algorithm is polynomial time?
options: No; it describes finite measurements only.
Yes; any plotted fit is a proof.
check.explanation: Many different functions can fit finite noisy samples. Count operations to establish asymptotic behavior.

lessons.python:
# Plot-ready data; no plotting package is required to run this example.
ns = [100, 200, 400, 800]
ts_ms = [1, 2, 4, 8]
points = list(zip(ns, ts_ms))
ratio = ts_ms[2] / ts_ms[1]
scale = 0.01
predicted_ms = [scale*n for n in ns]
# A curve matching these samples need not predict unsampled sizes correctly.
alternative_ms = [scale*n + 1e-12*(n-100)*(n-200)*(n-400)*(n-800) for n in ns]
assert alternative_ms == predicted_ms
start, stop, count = 0, 1, 5
linspace = [start + i*(stop-start)/(count-1) for i in range(count)]
print(points, ratio, predicted_ms, linspace)

teaching.motivation: A graph can make scaling visible, but an attractive fitted curve can also give unjustified confidence about unmeasured inputs.
teaching.background: A timing plot pairs each input size on the horizontal axis with its measured time on the vertical axis. Ratios and model curves summarize those pairs. Fitting is descriptive: many functions can agree at a finite set of points and disagree sharply outside it.
teaching.objective: Interpret paired timing data, compare doubling behavior and explain why extrapolation needs theoretical support.
applications: A benchmark chart helps compare how two implementations respond as the workload grows.
Checking a model against new sizes can expose a curve that merely overfit the original samples.
teaching.summary: The illustrative data doubled with n and matched a scaled linear model. Another function could match the same samples, so a fitted curve alone did not establish future growth or machine-independent runtime.
teaching.next: Counting primitive operations and identifying dominant terms provide the missing theoretical constraints.
bridges: Pair sizes [100,200,400,800] with illustrative times [1,2,4,8] milliseconds. Each plotted point must preserve that positional correspondence.
Comparing adjacent sizes shows a time ratio of two when size doubles. That pattern is consistent with a linear model for these samples, rather than proof of one for all sizes.
The model 0.01*n reproduces the illustrated milliseconds. Its scale factor converts an operation-growth idea into a prediction for this particular unit and environment.
The alternative curve in the code passes through the same samples yet can differ elsewhere. This demonstrates why more flexible fitting can hide rather than resolve uncertainty.
The final sampling example selects five evenly spaced points from zero through one. Choose sampling and plot coordinates deliberately before interpreting the shape of a chart.

lessons.title: Input size and counting primitive work
lessons.invariant: Count executions consistently under the stated cost model.
lessons.complexity: A loop doing fixed work n times is Theta(n).
lessons.takeaway: Write a cost function before discarding constants.

steps.caption: Define the size parameter
steps.why: Here n is the number of loop iterations, not the numeric magnitude of the sum.

steps.caption: Count initialization once
steps.why: A constant setup cost does not depend on n.

steps.caption: Count the repeated body
steps.why: The addition and update occur once per element.

steps.caption: Form a symbolic sum
steps.why: Different primitive counts can change constants while preserving linear growth.

steps.caption: State the input and arithmetic assumptions
steps.why: For huge integer magnitudes, arithmetic cost is not constant; use the model appropriate to the problem.

check.question: Why can two correct analyses count different constants?
check.explanation: A consistent cost model may group tests or assignments differently while yielding the same asymptotic class.

lessons.python:
n = 4
total = 0
body_executions = 0
for x in range(n):
    total += x
    body_executions += 1
a, b = 2, 3
unit_cost_model = a*n + b
large_operand = 10**100
operand_bits = large_operand.bit_length()
assert body_executions == n
print(total, unit_cost_model, operand_bits)

teaching.motivation: To predict runtime without depending on a particular stopwatch, we need to identify what grows and count how often meaningful operations execute.
teaching.background: An input-size parameter describes the aspect of the problem being varied. A cost model assigns work to basic operations. Summing execution counts produces a symbolic cost function; treating arithmetic as constant work assumes bounded-size operands or an explicitly simplified unit-cost model.
teaching.objective: Define n, count loop work and derive a cost expression with its assumptions stated.
applications: A scan analysis counts comparisons as the number of stored records grows.
Analyzing large-number arithmetic separately prevents a constant-time arithmetic assumption from hiding increasing operand size.
teaching.summary: Initialization ran once, the body ran n times, and the resulting model had a linear repeated term plus fixed overhead. The claim depended on what n meant and on which operations were treated as constant cost.
teaching.next: Dominant-term analysis simplifies the cost function, while case analysis describes how different inputs of one size change its work.
bridges: Here n=4 means four iterations of range(n), not the final numeric sum. Fixing that meaning makes the subsequent counts unambiguous.
The initialization total=0 executes once before repetition begins. The diagram separates that fixed setup from tests and body executions.
The body visits 0,1,2,3 and updates total once per value. Those four visits are the source of the n-dependent cost.
Writing a*n+b collects repeated work into a linear term and one-time work into an overhead term. Different reasonable primitive-operation groupings can change a and b.
The last diagram distinguishes iteration count from operand bit length. Very large integers can make arithmetic itself variable-cost, so the model must state that assumption.

lessons.title: Best, worst and average cases
lessons.source: Slide 2 pp4,9,13-14,19; corrects shorthand that equates bounds with cases.
lessons.invariant: Compare inputs of the same size before selecting a case function.
lessons.complexity: Linear search: best Theta(1), worst Theta(n); average requires a distribution.
lessons.takeaway: A case selects inputs; a bound describes the resulting cost function.

steps.caption: Fix n=5 and the search procedure
steps.why: The algorithm scans left to right and stops at the first match.
steps.code:
for x in a:
    if x == target: return True

steps.caption: Best case: target first
steps.why: Only one comparison is needed even though the list contains five items.

steps.caption: Worst case: target absent
steps.why: All five items must be checked before failure can be concluded.

steps.caption: Average case needs assumptions
steps.why: With a uniformly chosen successful position, the mean comparison count is (n+1)/2.

steps.caption: Do not confuse cases with bounds
steps.why: The worst-case cost n is both O(n) and Omega(n), hence Theta(n).

check.question: Can a worst-case runtime have an Omega(n) lower bound?
options: Yes. Bounds and cases are different axes.
No. Omega always means best case.
check.explanation: Omega gives a lower bound on the chosen cost function, including a worst-case function.

lessons.python:
def comparisons(a, target):
    count = 0
    for value in a:
        count += 1
        if value == target:
            return count
    return count
a = [8, 2, 7, 4, 6]
best = comparisons(a, 8)
worst = comparisons(a, 9)
successful_costs = [comparisons(a, target) for target in a]
average = sum(successful_costs) / len(a)
assert best == 1 and worst == len(a) and average == 3
# The worst-case function n has both O(n) and Omega(n) bounds.
print(best, worst, average)

teaching.motivation: Two searches over equally long lists can take different times because the target appears at different positions or is absent.
teaching.background: Case analysis first fixes an input size and then studies a minimum, maximum or expected cost over inputs of that size. Expected cost needs a probability distribution. O, Omega and Theta instead describe bounds on whichever cost function has been selected.
teaching.objective: Separate best, worst and average-case functions from upper, lower and tight bounds.
applications: A user-facing search may need a worst-case latency guarantee even if typical matches occur early.
A probabilistic workload model can estimate expected comparisons when successful target positions are uniformly distributed.
teaching.summary: With five positions, finding the first item cost one comparison and proving absence cost five. An average of three came from a stated successful-position distribution, not from the word Theta.
teaching.next: The three asymptotic-bound lessons compare growth of these case functions without changing which inputs they describe.
bridges: Use the fixed list [8,2,7,4,6] and keep n=5 while changing only the target. This isolates variation caused by the input case.
Searching for eight succeeds at the first cell, so the counter is one. Increasing the unused suffix would not change this best-case path.
Searching for nine finds no match, so every cell must be inspected. The highlighted entire list explains the worst-case count of five.
If each successful position is equally likely, average the costs 1,2,3,4,5 to obtain three. A different probability model could produce a different expected cost.
The worst-case function n has both an upper and a lower linear bound. The final diagram makes clear that choosing worst case and choosing O or Omega are independent decisions.

lessons.title: Dominant terms and asymptotic growth
lessons.invariant: For sufficiently large n, a fixed positive leading term dominates lower-order terms.
lessons.complexity: 2*n+3 is Theta(n); n^2+100*n is Theta(n^2).
lessons.takeaway: Dropping constants describes growth, not exact elapsed time.

steps.caption: Evaluate a cost function
steps.why: Small inputs can be affected strongly by constant overhead.

steps.caption: Compare T(n) with n
steps.why: The ratio approaches a positive constant as n grows.

steps.caption: Drop fixed factors for growth class
steps.why: A factor of two still matters in practice, but does not change the linear class.

steps.caption: Compare terms of different degree
steps.why: The quadratic term eventually dominates even when the linear coefficient is large.

steps.caption: Keep practical interpretation
steps.why: Asymptotic dominance does not identify the fastest implementation for every small input.

check.question: What is the tight growth class of 3*n^2 + 50*n + 7?
check.explanation: The positive quadratic term dominates the lower-order linear and constant terms.

lessons.python:
ns = [1, 10, 100]
costs = [2*n + 3 for n in ns]
ratios = [cost/n for cost,n in zip(costs,ns)]
linear_factors = [1, 2, 50]
linear_at_100 = [factor*100 for factor in linear_factors]
quadratic_to_linear_ratio = [n/100 for n in [10,100,1000]]
assert quadratic_to_linear_ratio[-1] > 1
# Growth classes discard constants; measured performance must still consider them.
print(costs, ratios, linear_at_100, quadratic_to_linear_ratio)

teaching.motivation: Exact instruction counts are useful, but we also need a way to compare algorithms without being distracted by every fixed setup cost.
teaching.background: Asymptotic analysis describes growth for sufficiently large inputs. Fixed positive factors and lower-order terms do not change a tight growth class. This simplification does not erase their effect on actual performance for finite inputs.
teaching.objective: Identify dominant terms while preserving the distinction between growth class and exact runtime.
applications: Comparing n^2 with n log n can expose a scaling problem that small benchmark inputs conceal.
Keeping constants in practical benchmarks still matters when choosing among implementations in the same growth class.
teaching.summary: The ratio (2n+3)/n approached two, establishing why that expression behaves linearly. A quadratic term eventually dominates a large linear term, but the crossover still matters for a real workload.
teaching.next: Big-O, Omega and Theta formalize these eventual comparisons with explicit scaling constants and thresholds.
bridges: Evaluate 2*n+3 at n=1,10,100. The constant three is a substantial fraction of the first result but a much smaller fraction of the last.
Divide each cost by n to isolate relative growth. The displayed ratios approach two because the extra 3/n becomes smaller.
Now compare n,2*n,50*n. Their scale factors differ, but each grows proportionally to n, which is what a shared linear class records.
For n^2+100*n, compare the two terms through their ratio n/100. Once n is large enough, the quadratic term drives further growth.
The final decision diagram restores the practical context: growth helps predict scaling, while constants and actual input sizes still affect which implementation is faster today.

lessons.title: Big-O: eventual upper bounds
lessons.source: Slide 2 pages 8-12; definitions clarify slide shorthand about cases.
lessons.invariant: For all n >= n0, f(n) <= c*g(n), for some c > 0.
lessons.complexity: Bounds describe functions, not input-case names.
lessons.takeaway: A upper bound becomes useful when its comparison function and threshold are stated.

steps.caption: Choose f(n)=2*n+3
steps.why: A bound is a statement about growth after some threshold.

steps.caption: Propose g(n)=n and c=4
steps.why: The candidate upper envelope is 4*n.

steps.caption: Check the threshold
steps.why: At n=2, f=7 <=8; the inequality continues because 2*n+3 <=4*n for n>=2.

steps.caption: Conclude an upper bound
steps.why: O(n) need not be the only true bound: O(n^2) is also true but looser.

steps.caption: Select a case separately
steps.why: The bound can describe best, average or worst-case cost, depending on which f was chosen.

check.question: What does this notation describe?
options: An eventual upper bound on a chosen cost function
check.explanation: Asymptotic notation compares growth after a threshold. Case analysis chooses the cost function being bounded.

lessons.python:
def f(n):
    return 2*n + 3
def g(n):
    return n
c, n0 = 4, 2
# Algebraic justification: n>=2 implies 3<=2n, so 2n+3<=4n.
assert f(n0) <= c*g(n0)
for n in range(n0, 101):
    assert f(n) <= c*g(n)
    assert f(n) <= c*n*n
# Finite assertions illustrate, rather than prove, the all-n algebraic bound.
worst_cost = lambda n: n
assert worst_cost(10) <= c*g(10)
print('Upper bounds apply to a chosen cost function.')

teaching.motivation: We often need to argue that an algorithm does not grow faster than a manageable comparison function beyond some input size.
teaching.background: Big-O is an eventual upper bound. To show f(n)=O(g(n)), choose a positive constant c and threshold n0 such that f(n)<=c*g(n) for every n>=n0. The bound may be loose, and it can describe any selected best, average or worst-case function.
teaching.objective: Construct a valid upper-bound witness and distinguish an upper bound from an exact growth claim.
applications: An algorithm specification can promise at most linear growth in a defined worst-case operation count.
A loose polynomial bound can still rule out exponential behavior even before a tighter analysis is known.
teaching.summary: For f(n)=2n+3, choosing c=4 and n0=2 placed every later value below 4n. That proved O(n), while O(n^2) remained true but less informative.
teaching.next: A matching Omega bound is needed to conclude the tight class Theta(n).
bridges: Begin with the cost function 2*n+3. We are bounding this function, not measuring exact seconds or choosing an input case.
Try g(n)=n and scale it by four. The diagram constructs the proposed upper envelope before asking where it becomes valid.
At n=2, seven is below eight; algebra then shows 2*n+3<=4*n for every n>=2. Sample checks illustrate that reasoning but do not replace the all-n argument.
The linear envelope establishes O(n). The quadratic envelope also works eventually, which is why saying only Big-O does not automatically promise the tightest bound.
Finally, choose which case function you want to bound. A worst-case count can have this O(n) bound, but the notation itself does not mean worst case.

lessons.title: Big-Omega: eventual lower bounds
lessons.source: Slide 2 pages 13; definitions clarify slide shorthand about cases.
lessons.invariant: For all n >= n0, f(n) >= c*g(n), for some c > 0.
lessons.complexity: Bounds describe functions, not input-case names.
lessons.takeaway: A lower bound becomes useful when its comparison function and threshold are stated.

steps.caption: Choose f(n)=2*n+3
steps.why: A lower bound says the cost cannot grow more slowly than a scaled comparison function.

steps.caption: Propose g(n)=n and c=2
steps.why: 2*n is no greater than 2*n+3 for positive n.

steps.caption: Compare at n=3
steps.why: The lower envelope 6 lies below the actual cost 9.

steps.caption: Conclude Omega(n)
steps.why: A lower bound can be loose: Omega(1) is also true here.

steps.caption: Keep the case separate
steps.why: A worst-case function can have an Omega bound; Omega is not a synonym for best case.

check.question: What does this notation describe?
options: An eventual lower bound on a chosen cost function
check.explanation: Asymptotic notation compares growth after a threshold. Case analysis chooses the cost function being bounded.

lessons.python:
def f(n):
    return 2*n + 3
def g(n):
    return n
c, n0 = 2, 1
# Algebraic justification: 2n <= 2n+3 for every n>=1.
assert c*g(3) <= f(3)
for n in range(n0, 101):
    assert c*g(n) <= f(n)
    assert 1 <= f(n)
worst_cost = lambda n: n
assert 1*10 <= worst_cost(10)
print('Lower bounds are independent of case selection.')

teaching.motivation: An upper bound alone does not say how much work is unavoidable; a lower bound captures growth that the chosen cost function cannot fall below.
teaching.background: Big-Omega is an eventual lower bound: f(n)>=c*g(n) for some positive c and all n beyond a threshold. It applies to a selected function, not automatically to best-case behavior. A true lower bound may still be weaker than the tightest one.
teaching.objective: Give a lower-bound witness and explain why it is independent of input-case selection.
applications: A full-input aggregation has a linear lower bound when each input item must influence the result.
Lower bounds help show that an implementation already matches the unavoidable growth for a chosen problem model.
teaching.summary: The function 2n+3 stayed above 2n, so Omega(n) described its unavoidable linear growth. Omega(1) was also true but weaker; neither statement selected best-case inputs.
teaching.next: Combining a linear lower bound with a linear upper bound yields Theta(n).
bridges: Use the same 2*n+3 function so the direction of the bound is the only change from the upper-bound lesson. We now seek an envelope below it.
Choose g(n)=n and c=2. Because the constant three is nonnegative, 2*n lies below the target for all positive n.
At n=3, the diagram compares six with nine. This concrete point helps interpret the algebraic inequality rather than serving as its entire proof.
Omega(n) captures the linear lower growth. Omega(1) also holds, but describing only a constant lower bound leaves useful information unstated.
Apply the same reasoning to worst(n)=n. Its Omega(n) bound is valid even though it is a worst-case function, demonstrating that bounds and cases answer different questions.

lessons.title: Big-Theta: matching lower and upper bounds
lessons.source: Slide 2 pages 14; definitions clarify slide shorthand about cases.
lessons.invariant: For n >= n0, c1*g(n) <= f(n) <= c2*g(n), with c1,c2 > 0.
lessons.complexity: Bounds describe functions, not input-case names.
lessons.takeaway: A tight bound becomes useful when its comparison function and threshold are stated.

steps.caption: Choose f(n)=2*n+3
steps.why: A tight asymptotic bound requires both sides.

steps.caption: Sandwich the function
steps.why: At n=10, the cost 23 lies between 20 and 40.

steps.caption: Conclude Theta(n)
steps.why: Theta is tight growth; it does not mean average case or exact equality.

check.question: What does this notation describe?
options: An eventual tight bound on a chosen cost function
check.explanation: Asymptotic notation compares growth after a threshold. Case analysis chooses the cost function being bounded.

lessons.python:
def f(n):
    return 2*n + 3
c1, c2, n0 = 2, 4, 2
# For all n>=2, 2n <= 2n+3 <= 4n follows algebraically.
for n in range(n0, 101):
    assert c1*n <= f(n)
    assert f(n) <= c2*n
assert 20 <= f(10) <= 40
print('f(n) is Theta(n), a tight growth bound.')

teaching.motivation: When upper and lower analyses agree in growth, we can describe a cost more precisely than by saying it is merely no larger than some function.
teaching.background: Big-Theta gives an eventual two-sided bound: positive constant multiples of g(n) lie below and above f(n). It describes proportional growth up to constants, not exact equality, elapsed seconds or average-case behavior.
teaching.objective: Establish a tight bound by combining matching upper and lower envelopes.
applications: A complete scan that does constant work per item is tightly linear rather than merely bounded above by a quadratic function.
A tight analysis lets us compare expected scaling without claiming machine-specific running times.
teaching.summary: The function 2n+3 was squeezed between 2n and 4n after n=2. Both sides had linear growth, so Theta(n) expressed the matching result.
teaching.next: Growth-class comparisons use tight bounds to explain why logarithmic, linear and quadratic procedures scale differently.
bridges: Start again with 2*n+3 and propose n as its comparison function. A tight claim will need evidence on both sides.
The lower envelope 2*n cannot exceed the target because the target has an extra positive three. This supplies one half of the desired sandwich.
For n>=2, 4*n is an upper envelope. The same threshold can now support both inequalities at once.
At n=10, the values 20,23,40 make the sandwich visible. The actual cost need not equal n or either envelope.
The two linear bounds together justify Theta(n). The conclusion describes tight growth of the selected function, with its input case still specified separately.

lessons.title: Constant, logarithmic, linear and faster growth
lessons.source: Slide 2 pp15-17,23-24; 02-timing cell31 for n log n and exponential comparison.
lessons.invariant: Compare costs using the same n and unit-cost model.
lessons.complexity: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n^2 < 2^n eventually.
lessons.takeaway: Doubling patterns reveal why input scale changes feasibility.

steps.caption: Constant work
steps.why: A fixed number of bounded-cost operations does not grow with n.

steps.caption: Halve a remaining interval
steps.why: Repeated halving requires about log2(n) steps.

steps.caption: Visit every item once
steps.why: Doubling n doubles a full scan.

steps.caption: Visit every pair
steps.why: Two independent n-iteration loops visit n*n pairs.
steps.code:
for x in a:
    for y in a: use(x,y)

steps.caption: Compare linearithmic and exponential
steps.why: Merge-style n log n grows much slower than doubling a recursion tree at each level.

check.question: If n doubles, how does n^2 change?

lessons.python:
import math
constant = [1 for n in [8, 16]]
remaining = 16
halving_trace = [remaining]
while remaining > 1:
    remaining //= 2
    halving_trace.append(remaining)
scan_work = [n for n in [8,16,32]]
pair_work = [n*n for n in [8,16,32]]
n = 16
comparison = [n*math.log2(n), n*n, 2**n]
print(constant, halving_trace, scan_work, pair_work, comparison)

teaching.motivation: Scaling input by a factor of two can add one step, double work, quadruple it or cause a much larger increase, depending on the algorithm.
teaching.background: A growth class summarizes how modeled work depends on input size. Constant work stays fixed; logarithmic work repeatedly reduces the problem by a factor; scans are linear; all-pairs work is quadratic. Combining linear work with logarithmic levels gives n log n, while branching can yield exponential work.
teaching.objective: Relate common code patterns and doubling behavior to their growth classes.
applications: A midpoint search can remain practical on large sorted collections because each comparison halves the remaining interval.
Checking every pair of records can become infeasible far sooner than checking each record once.
teaching.summary: The diagrams connected fixed work, repeated halving, full scans and pair enumeration to their distinct scaling. At n=16, the n log n, n^2 and 2^n values illustrated how quickly those differences become significant.
teaching.next: Search, sorting and recursion lessons show these growth patterns arising from complete algorithms.
bridges: The first comparison performs the same fixed work for sizes eight and sixteen. Constant time describes independence from n, not a guarantee that the operation takes literally one machine instruction.
The remaining interval shrinks 16,8,4,2,1. Each halving needs one more stage, explaining logarithmic rather than linear growth.
A full scan must visit each of 8,16,32 items. Unlike halving, doubling n doubles the number of visits.
Two independent loops consider every ordered pair. Squaring 8,16,32 produces 64,256,1024, so doubling size now multiplies work by four.
The final n=16 comparison puts 64,256,65536 side by side. Those n log n, quadratic and exponential values explain why identifying the growth pattern matters before scaling an application.

lessons.title: The list ADT: order, positions and operations
lessons.invariant: The logical list is an ordered sequence independent of how it is stored.
lessons.complexity: Costs vary by implementation even when list behavior is identical.
lessons.takeaway: An index identifies a position; duplicates do not break the list model.

steps.caption: Store an ordered sequence
steps.why: Order is part of list behavior, unlike abstract set membership.

steps.caption: Access by position
steps.why: Two equal values still occupy different positions.

steps.caption: Replace one item
steps.why: Replacement preserves length and all other positions.

steps.caption: Insert an item
steps.why: Insertion changes length and the logical positions of following items.

steps.caption: Delete and concatenate
steps.why: Deletion closes a logical gap; concatenation preserves each operand order.

check.question: Does replacing items[1] change the list length?
options: No. Replacement keeps the same positions.
check.explanation: Index assignment changes a stored value, whereas insertion adds a position.

lessons.python:
items = [7, 7, 2]
assert len(items) == 3
assert items[1] == 7
items[1] = 9
items.insert(1, 5)
assert items == [7, 5, 9, 2]
del items[1]
items = items + [8]
assert items == [7, 9, 2, 8]
print(items)

teaching.motivation: Applications often need an ordered collection that supports reading, replacing, adding and removing items without losing track of their positions.
teaching.background: A list is an ordered sequence, so equal values can occupy different positions. Access retrieves an existing position; replacement changes its value; insertion and deletion change the number and positions of items. These behaviors define the contract before a storage implementation is chosen.
teaching.objective: Predict how list operations affect values, order, positions and length.
applications: A playlist needs positional order and can contain the same song more than once.
Editing a sequence of measurements requires distinguishing replacement of one reading from insertion of another.
teaching.summary: The example preserved list order while replacing, inserting and deleting values. Concatenation then created a sequence containing the left operand followed by the right, demonstrating that logical behavior is separate from storage cost.
teaching.next: Array and linked implementations satisfy this contract with different access and update mechanisms.
bridges: Begin with [7,7,2]. The repeated sevens occupy separate positions, so a list represents more than unique membership.
Position one identifies the second seven. The selected cell explains why an index denotes a place even when neighboring values compare equal.
Replacing that position with nine changes a value but keeps length three. No later element needs a new logical index.
Inserting five at position one creates a new place between seven and nine. The following items move to later logical positions and length becomes four.
Deleting five closes that logical gap; concatenating [8] then adds the right-hand sequence after all remaining left-hand items. Follow the code order to obtain [7,9,2,8].

lessons.title: Arrays: contiguous slots and direct indexing
lessons.source: Slide 3 pp4-5; 03-array-list cells4-13. Slots may store references rather than inline object payloads.
lessons.invariant: Slot i is located using base + i*slot_size within the allocated capacity.
lessons.complexity: Valid index access and replacement O(1); allocating/copying n slots O(n).
lessons.takeaway: Array length is fixed; a dynamic list manages a separate logical size.

steps.caption: Allocate four slots
steps.why: An array has a fixed allocated number of slots in this model.

steps.caption: Store three logical items
steps.why: An unused slot is capacity, not part of the logical list.

steps.caption: Compute the address of index 2
steps.why: Direct arithmetic identifies a slot without following prior elements.

steps.caption: Replace a value in place
steps.why: Replacing a valid item does not change size or capacity.

steps.caption: Distinguish fixed arrays from array lists
steps.why: A list wrapper can allocate another array when needed; the original array does not stretch.

check.question: Why is array indexing O(1) in this model?
options: A slot address is computed directly.
check.explanation: The base address and fixed slot size locate an item without traversing earlier slots.

lessons.python:
base, slot_bytes, capacity = 100, 8, 4
addresses = [base+i*slot_bytes for i in range(capacity)]
storage = [None]*capacity
storage[:3] = [4,9,2]
size = 3
i = 2
address = base+i*slot_bytes
assert address == 116
storage[i] = 7
logical_list = storage[:size]
assert logical_list == [4,9,7] and len(storage) == capacity
print(addresses, storage, size, capacity)

teaching.motivation: Fast access to an arbitrary position is possible when storage has a regular layout rather than requiring a walk through earlier items.
teaching.background: An array allocates a fixed number of equally sized slots. Given a base address and slot size, arithmetic locates slot i. A dynamic list built on an array separately tracks logical size and allocated capacity; unused capacity is not part of the logical sequence.
teaching.objective: Explain direct indexing and distinguish fixed allocated capacity from the number of stored list items.
applications: A table of samples benefits from constant-time access to a known measurement index.
A dynamic-list wrapper can reserve extra slots to support future appends without allocating on every update.
teaching.summary: The address example located index two directly, then replaced its value without changing allocation. Keeping size three separate from capacity four explained how a fixed array can underlie a growable list.
teaching.next: Capacity doubling addresses what happens when every reserved slot is occupied.
bridges: Allocate four slots beginning at address 100 with eight bytes per slot. The diagram shows regularly spaced addresses rather than a chain of references to traverse.
Only three slots hold logical values [4,9,2]. The remaining blank is reserved capacity, so size and capacity are already different.
For index two, compute 100+2*8=116. The highlighted address demonstrates why reaching that slot does not require inspecting indices zero and one.
Writing seven into that position replaces the old two in place. The allocation and logical length remain unchanged.
The final size=3 and cap=4 boxes name the two layers of bookkeeping. A wrapper may later allocate another array, but this existing array does not physically stretch.

lessons.title: Singly and doubly linked list structure
lessons.invariant: Following next preserves list order; doubly linked neighbors agree in both directions.
lessons.complexity: Traversal O(n); a doubly linked node uses another link per node.
lessons.takeaway: More links permit backward navigation but require more maintenance.

steps.caption: A node holds a value and a link
steps.why: Links store relationships; nodes need not occupy adjacent memory addresses.

steps.caption: A head identifies the first node
steps.why: A singly linked list begins at head and ends with next=None.

steps.caption: Access requires traversal
