steps.why: Without a direct node reference, reaching position 2 follows two next links.
steps.code:
node = head
for _ in range(2): node = node.next

steps.caption: Add predecessor references
steps.why: A doubly linked list adds prev pointers, enabling backward travel.

steps.caption: Maintain both directions
steps.why: Inserting X between A and B must update both neighboring links and X fields.

check.question: What extra relationship does a doubly linked node store?
options: An array index for every node
A sorted copy of the list
check.explanation: The prev reference permits backward navigation and adds maintenance obligations.

lessons.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None
        self.prev = None
A, B, C = [Node(v) for v in ['A','B','C']]
A.next, B.next = B, C
head = A
node = head
for _ in range(2):
    node = node.next
assert node is C
B.prev, C.prev = A, B
X = Node('X')
A.next, X.prev = X, A
X.next, B.prev = B, X
assert A.next is X and X.next is B and B.prev is X
print(head.value, X.value, node.value)

teaching.motivation: When sequence updates should change relationships rather than shift stored items, a chain of nodes offers a different representation from an array.
teaching.background: A linked node stores a value and references to neighboring nodes. head reaches the first node, and None marks an absent neighbor. Singly linked nodes store next; doubly linked nodes add prev, allowing backward navigation but requiring both directions to remain consistent.
teaching.objective: Trace a linked representation and identify the fields needed for traversal and insertion.
applications: A linked sequence can prepend an item by changing references instead of shifting an entire array.
A doubly linked navigation history can move both backward and forward through neighboring records.
teaching.summary: The head and next fields established forward order, while prev added backward navigation. Inserting X between A and B required maintaining both neighbors, showing the bookkeeping cost of that extra flexibility.
teaching.next: Linked update and reversal lessons perform these reference changes step by step.
bridges: Inspect one node containing value four and a next reference to B. The value is data; the reference determines where traversal continues.
Starting at head A, follow next through B and C until None. This chain defines logical order even if the objects are not adjacent in memory.
To access position two, traverse two links from head. The highlighted C demonstrates why linked indexing cannot use array-style address arithmetic.
Adding prev to B and C provides reverse links to their predecessors. The diagram now records two directions for each neighboring pair.
Insert X between A and B by updating A.next, X.prev, X.next and B.prev. Maintaining only the forward half would leave the doubly linked structure inconsistent.

lessons.title: Choosing arrays or linked lists by operation cost
lessons.source: Slide 3 pp6,13-17; 05-linked-list cells12-15. Append qualifiers are implementation-specific.
lessons.invariant: Include the cost of locating a position before changing links.
lessons.complexity: Array access O(1); linked access O(n); linked head insertion O(1).
lessons.takeaway: A cheap pointer update does not make arbitrary-position deletion constant time.

steps.caption: Compare the same logical values
steps.why: The representation is what changes operation costs.

steps.caption: An array indexes directly
steps.why: The requested position can be reached using address arithmetic.

steps.caption: A linked list follows links
steps.why: Finding index 3 from head requires traversing earlier nodes.

steps.caption: Prepending favors the linked head
steps.why: The array shifts items; a linked list updates two references.

steps.caption: Append depends on stored endpoints
steps.why: A tail pointer makes linked append O(1); the course head-only implementation walks to the end.

check.question: Why can linked deletion by index take O(n)?
options: Finding the predecessor may require traversal.
Reassigning a pointer is always O(n).
All linked lists copy the whole list.
check.explanation: Once the predecessor is known, the link update is O(1); locating it can dominate.

lessons.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next_node=None):
        self.value, self.next = value, next_node
values = [10,20,30,40]
array_value = values[3]
head = None
for value in reversed(values):
    head = Node(value,head)
node = head
for _ in range(3):
    node = node.next
assert node.value == array_value
head = Node(5,head)
tail = node
tail.next = Node(50)
tail = tail.next
print(head.value, tail.value)

teaching.motivation: Choosing a list representation by the word list alone can hide major differences between indexing, prepending and appending costs.
teaching.background: Arrays locate indexed slots directly but shift items for some positional updates. Linked lists walk references to locate positions but can rewire known neighbors cheaply. Stored endpoint references also matter: a tail pointer changes append from a traversal into a local update.
teaching.objective: Compare operation costs using both the representation and the references already available.
applications: A read-heavy table with frequent random indexing often benefits from array access.
A queue implemented with linked head and tail references avoids walking the entire list on each enqueue.
teaching.summary: The same four values had constant-time array access but a linked traversal for index three. Linked prepend avoided shifting, and linked append became constant-time only after a tail reference was available.
teaching.next: Dynamic-array amortization and linked-list updates provide the detailed mechanisms behind these comparisons.
bridges: Keep [10,20,30,40] fixed while comparing two implementations. Changing the data would obscure which differences come from representation.
The array reads position three directly. Its highlighted last cell is reached without checking the preceding values.
The linked version begins at head and follows three links to the same forty. Include that locating work in the access cost.
Prepending five reverses the advantage: a linked head update is local, while an array would move the existing suffix. The diagram shows the same resulting logical order.
Finally, store a tail reference and attach fifty there. Without that endpoint, the code would first need another walk from head.

lessons.title: Linear search: scan until a match
lessons.invariant: Every position before i has been ruled out.
lessons.complexity: Best Theta(1); worst Theta(n); iterative auxiliary space O(1).
lessons.takeaway: Stop on a match; scan the entire input to prove absence.

steps.caption: Search an unsorted sequence
steps.why: No ordering assumption is needed; start with no positions eliminated.

steps.caption: Compare index 0: 14 with 9
steps.why: Earlier positions have already been checked.

steps.caption: Compare index 1: 7 with 9
steps.why: Earlier positions have already been checked.

steps.caption: Compare index 2: 22 with 9
steps.why: Earlier positions have already been checked.

steps.caption: Compare index 3: 9 with 9
steps.why: Equality proves membership, so later positions do not need checking.

steps.caption: Return True after four comparisons
steps.why: If no comparison matched, only reaching the end would justify returning False.

check.question: When must linear search inspect every item?
options: Only when the target is first.
check.explanation: An absent target cannot be ruled out until all items have been examined.

teaching.motivation: An unsorted collection offers no reliable half to discard, so a membership procedure may need to examine records one by one.
teaching.background: Linear search compares a target with each element in sequence and stops at a match. Its useful invariant is that all earlier positions have been ruled out. Failure is justified only after the entire sequence has been checked.
teaching.objective: Trace successful and unsuccessful linear search and explain why absence requires a full scan.
applications: A short unsorted list of allowed settings can be checked without building an index.
Searching linked nodes for a matching value naturally follows their sequence one node at a time.
teaching.summary: The target nine appeared after three failures, so the search returned True after four comparisons. Earlier failures justified moving forward; a match justified stopping before the remaining two values.
teaching.next: Binary search can eliminate larger regions when sortedness supplies additional information.
bridges: Search [14,7,22,9,31,4] for nine. No sorted-order promise is available, so the loop starts with every position as a candidate.
Fourteen differs from nine, ruling out only index zero. The highlighted comparison and counter show why the search must continue.
Seven also differs, so the ruled-out prefix now includes two positions. No conclusion follows about values farther to the right.
Twenty-two is another mismatch. The first three positions are finished, but their values cannot prove where nine might be.
At index three, the comparison succeeds. Equality establishes membership immediately, so neither 31 nor 4 needs inspection.
Return True with four comparisons completed. If every comparison had failed, the loop ending would instead justify False.

lessons.title: Binary search with index bounds
lessons.invariant: If the target exists, it lies in the remaining sorted interval.
lessons.complexity: Worst O(log n) comparisons; iterative O(1) space; recursive O(log n) stack.
lessons.takeaway: Halve an index interval; repeated Python list slices add copying costs.

steps.caption: Use sorted input and inclusive bounds
steps.why: Sortedness is the reason an entire half can be eliminated.

steps.caption: Inspect midpoint 4: value 16
steps.why: All remaining candidate positions lie between low and high.

steps.caption: Discard the impossible half
steps.why: The midpoint and all smaller values to its left cannot equal the larger target.

steps.caption: Inspect midpoint 6: value 38
steps.why: All remaining candidate positions lie between low and high.

steps.caption: Discard the impossible half
steps.why: The midpoint and all larger values to its right cannot equal the smaller target.

steps.caption: Inspect midpoint 5: value 23
steps.why: All remaining candidate positions lie between low and high.

steps.caption: Found 23 at index 5
steps.why: Equality is the success condition; an empty interval would be failure.

check.question: Why can the left half be discarded when a[mid] < target?
options: Sortedness makes every value there too small.
The midpoint is always the answer.
check.explanation: All positions at or left of mid have values <= a[mid], so none can equal a larger target.

teaching.motivation: A sorted collection lets one failed comparison eliminate many positions, making repeated searches far cheaper than scanning every item.
teaching.background: Binary search maintains a remaining interval in sorted data. A midpoint comparison either finds the target or proves that one entire half cannot contain it. Inclusive low and high bounds avoid allocating copied sublists, and each unsuccessful comparison strictly reduces the interval.
teaching.objective: Update inclusive bounds correctly and explain why each discarded region is impossible.
applications: A sorted catalog can locate an exact key using logarithmically many comparisons.
A monotone threshold problem can reuse interval-halving ideas once the ordering condition is established.
teaching.summary: The search ruled out values through 16, then values from 38 upward, leaving 23 alone at index five. Bounds preserved the original array and the invariant that any remaining match must lie inside the candidate interval.
teaching.next: Recursive binary search expresses the same shrinking interval through calls; index bounds avoid the extra copying of repeated Python slices.
bridges: Search the sorted nine-item array for 23 using inclusive bounds zero and eight. Sortedness is the reason future comparisons can rule out whole regions.
The midpoint is index four, holding 16. Since 16 is too small, every value to its left is also too small.
Set low to mid+1, which is five. The muted prefix shows that index four itself is excluded, ensuring the interval actually shrinks.
The new midpoint is index six, holding 38. This value and all values farther right are too large for target 23.
Set high to mid-1, leaving the single position five. The diagram makes the narrowed inclusive bounds visible.
Inspect index five and compare its value 23 with the target. Equality ends the search; no further interval reduction is required.
Return index five from the original array. The implementation changed bounds rather than slicing lists, so the logarithmic comparison argument is not hiding sublist-copy work.

lessons.title: Dynamic arrays: append and capacity doubling
lessons.invariant: The first size slots hold the logical list in order; size <= capacity.
lessons.complexity: Individual resize O(n); append amortized O(1); storage O(n).
lessons.takeaway: Doubling spends occasional linear work to keep a sequence of appends linear overall.

steps.caption: Capacity 4, logical size 3
steps.why: One reserved slot is unused; size and capacity answer different questions.

steps.caption: Append 8 without growing
steps.why: A free slot means one write and one size update suffice.

steps.caption: Appending 10 finds a full array
steps.why: A fixed-size backing array cannot accept another item without replacement.

steps.caption: Allocate double capacity
steps.why: The new array has enough spare slots to make future appends cheap.

steps.caption: Copy old item 0 into the same position
steps.why: Copying preserves logical order while moving to different storage.

steps.caption: Copy old item 1 into the same position
steps.why: Copying preserves logical order while moving to different storage.

steps.caption: Copy old item 2 into the same position
steps.why: Copying preserves logical order while moving to different storage.

steps.caption: Copy old item 3 into the same position
steps.why: Copying preserves logical order while moving to different storage.

steps.caption: Append 10 and replace the backing storage
steps.why: This append paid O(n) copying; spare slots make the next several appends O(1).

steps.caption: Spread resize cost across many appends
steps.why: Total copies 1+2+4+... are linear in the number of appended items; amortized is not a probability average.

check.question: Does amortized O(1) mean every append is O(1)?
options: No, one resize can copy n items.
check.explanation: Amortized analysis bounds total cost across a sequence, including expensive resize operations.

lessons.python:
storage = [2,4,6,None]
size, capacity = 3, 4
storage[size] = 8
size += 1
if size == capacity:
    new_capacity = 2*capacity
    new = [None]*new_capacity
    for i in range(size):
        new[i] = storage[i]
    storage, capacity = new, new_capacity
storage[size] = 10
size += 1
assert storage[:size] == [2,4,6,8,10]
copy_counts = [1,2,4,8]
assert sum(copy_counts) < 2*copy_counts[-1]
print(storage, size, capacity)

teaching.motivation: A fixed backing array eventually fills, but allocating and copying after every append would make building a list unnecessarily expensive.
teaching.background: A dynamic array tracks size and capacity separately. An append uses a free slot when possible; otherwise it allocates larger storage and copies existing items. Doubling leaves enough spare slots to spread occasional linear copying across many cheap appends, producing an amortized bound over a sequence.
teaching.objective: Trace a resize without changing order and explain amortized versus individual append cost.
applications: A growable list can accept a stream of records without knowing the final count in advance.
A text builder can reserve increasing capacity rather than reconstruct all earlier content on every addition.
teaching.summary: Appending eight used the existing free slot. Appending ten triggered doubling, four ordered copies and a final write. The expensive resize did not contradict amortized constant-time append because total copying across many doublings is linear.
teaching.next: Array insertion and deletion add shifting costs that spare capacity alone cannot remove.
bridges: The backing array has capacity four but only [2,4,6] is logically present. The blank fourth slot explains why the next append can avoid allocation.
Write eight into the reserved slot and increase size to four. This append performs no copies of old items.
Now ten has no available slot. Testing size==capacity identifies the point where an append needs more than a single write.
Allocate eight slots while retaining the old array as the copy source. The second row separates new reserved space from the still-valid old contents.
Copy the two at index zero into new index zero. Matching positions preserves the logical order across the storage change.
Copy four into new index one. The completed prefix grows while uncopied source values remain available.
Copy six into new index two. Every copied cell has the same value and position as before, despite living in another array.
Copy eight into new index three, finishing the old logical sequence. The remaining four slots are still reserved rather than list items.
Replace the backing reference, write ten at index four and set size to five. The diagram now shows one live array with three spare slots.

The final copy counts 1,2,4,8 form a geometric sum. Their total grows linearly with appended items, which is why occasional linear resizes can yield amortized constant cost without assuming random inputs.

lessons.title: Array-list prepend, insertion, deletion and concatenation
lessons.invariant: Shifting preserves the order of every item that remains.
lessons.complexity: Prepend/insert/delete worst O(n); concatenate lengths n,m in O(n+m).
lessons.takeaway: Shift right-to-left for insertion and left-to-right for deletion.

steps.caption: Start with four items and spare capacity
steps.why: Insertion changes logical positions, even when no allocation is needed.

steps.caption: Shift index 3 right before overwriting it
steps.why: Move right-to-left so an unread item is not destroyed.

steps.caption: Shift index 2 right before overwriting it
steps.why: Move right-to-left so an unread item is not destroyed.

steps.caption: Shift index 1 right before overwriting it
steps.why: Move right-to-left so an unread item is not destroyed.

steps.caption: Shift index 0 right before overwriting it
steps.why: Move right-to-left so an unread item is not destroyed.

steps.caption: Write the prepended value
steps.why: Only now is slot 0 free to receive the new logical first item.

steps.caption: Insert 15 at index 2
steps.why: The same rightward shift applies only to the suffix beginning at index 2.

steps.caption: Delete index 2 by shifting the suffix left
steps.why: Deletion preserves relative order and leaves one unused slot at the end.
steps.code:
for j in range(2,size-1): storage[j]=storage[j+1]
size -= 1

steps.caption: Concatenate with another sequence
steps.why: A fresh output copies the left operand followed by the right operand.

check.question: Why shift right-to-left when inserting?
options: To avoid overwriting an unread value.
check.explanation: A left-to-right shift would overwrite the next source item before it is copied.

lessons.python:
storage = [10,20,30,40,None,None]
size = 4
for i in range(size-1,-1,-1):
    storage[i+1] = storage[i]
storage[0] = 5
size += 1
position = 2
for i in range(size-1,position-1,-1):
    storage[i+1] = storage[i]
storage[position] = 15
size += 1
for j in range(position,size-1):
    storage[j] = storage[j+1]
size -= 1
storage[size] = None
left, right = storage[:size], [7,8]
combined = left + right
assert combined == [5,10,20,30,40,7,8]
print(combined)

teaching.motivation: An ordered array list must preserve positions when an item is inserted or deleted; extra capacity does not remove that ordering work.
teaching.background: Array insertion opens a gap by shifting a suffix right, and deletion closes a gap by shifting a suffix left. The copying direction matters because overwriting an unread source loses data. Concatenation creates an output containing both operand sequences in order.
teaching.objective: Perform safe shifts and relate the affected suffix to update cost.
applications: Prepending an urgent item to an array-backed ordered list requires moving existing items to later positions.
Removing a reading from the middle of a sample sequence preserves the order of every surviving reading.
teaching.summary: Moving from right to left safely opened space for five. The same mechanism inserted fifteen in the middle, deletion closed its gap, and concatenation copied the final sequence followed by seven and eight.
teaching.next: Linked lists preserve order through references instead, trading shifting costs for traversal and pointer bookkeeping.
bridges: Start with [10,20,30,40] and two spare slots, then request a prepend of five. The blank capacity makes allocation unnecessary, but logical positions still need to change.
Move forty from index three to four first. Starting at the right prevents the copied value from replacing an unread source.
Next move thirty from index two to three. The previously saved forty remains intact in its new slot.
Move twenty from index one to two. The right-to-left frontier separates items already moved from sources still needed.
Move ten from index zero to one. Only after this last shift is the first slot safe to overwrite.
Write five into index zero and increase size. The logical list is now [5,10,20,30,40] in the required order.
Insert fifteen at index two using the same rightward suffix shift. Only the suffix beginning at that position must move.
Delete index two and shift the later items left, restoring [5,10,20,30,40]. Left-to-right copying is safe for this opposite direction.
Concatenate the surviving left sequence with [7,8]. The third row records a fresh ordered result, so its copying cost includes both operands.

lessons.title: Linked-list prepend, append, access and deletion
lessons.invariant: Head reaches exactly the live sequence by next links.
lessons.complexity: Prepend O(1); head-only append/access/delete-by-index O(n).
lessons.takeaway: Separate locating a node from rewiring its links; a stored tail changes append cost.

steps.caption: Start at the head
steps.why: Only head is stored in this example; append will need a traversal.

steps.caption: Link a new node before head
steps.why: Set the new node link before changing head, preserving access to the old chain.

steps.caption: Make the new node the head
steps.why: Prepending changes only references, not the existing nodes.

steps.caption: Walk to the tail: current node 9
steps.why: A head-only singly linked list follows next references until next is None.
steps.code:
while current.next is not None:
    current = current.next

steps.caption: Walk to the tail: current node 1
steps.why: A head-only singly linked list follows next references until next is None.
steps.code:
while current.next is not None:
    current = current.next

steps.caption: Walk to the tail: current node 2
steps.why: A head-only singly linked list follows next references until next is None.
steps.code:
while current.next is not None:
    current = current.next

steps.caption: Walk to the tail: current node 3
steps.why: A head-only singly linked list follows next references until next is None.
steps.code:
while current.next is not None:
    current = current.next

steps.caption: Attach node 4 at the end
steps.why: Once the tail is found, the final append update is constant time.

steps.caption: Access zero-based index 2
steps.why: Start at head and follow two links; the result is node 2.

steps.caption: Delete node 2 using its predecessor
steps.why: Bypassing the target preserves the rest of the chain. Finding the predecessor can cost O(n).

steps.caption: The live list is now 9,1,3,4
steps.why: Deleting the head is the special case head=head.next; bounds and empty lists need checks.

check.question: How can a linked-list append be O(1)?
options: Use binary search on next links.
check.explanation: A stored tail avoids scanning from head; keep it correct when the list becomes empty.

lessons.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next_node=None):
        self.value, self.next = value, next_node
head = Node(1,Node(2,Node(3)))
new = Node(9)
new.next = head
head = new
current = head
while current.next is not None:
    current = current.next
current.next = Node(4)
accessed = head.next.next
assert accessed.value == 2
predecessor = head.next
predecessor.next = predecessor.next.next
values, current = [], head
while current is not None:
    values.append(current.value)
    current = current.next
assert values == [9,1,3,4]
print(values)

teaching.motivation: A linked list can add or remove a node by changing references, but the program must first have access to the correct neighboring nodes.
teaching.background: The head reference identifies the first singly linked node, and each next reference identifies its successor. Prepending is local; a head-only append must locate the tail. Deleting an interior node redirects its predecessor to its successor, while indexed access requires counting links.
teaching.objective: Separate traversal from local rewiring and preserve reachability during updates.
applications: A linked stack pushes at head without shifting an array suffix.
A linked queue stores a tail pointer so adding a new waiting job does not require a full traversal.
teaching.summary: The example prepended nine, walked to append four, located index two and bypassed that node. Local link changes were cheap, but locating endpoints or positions accounted for the linear costs.
teaching.next: List reversal and cycle detection depend on the same careful reasoning about which nodes remain reachable.
bridges: Begin with head pointing to 1 in the chain 1->2->3. No tail field is stored, so finding the end will require following next.
Create nine and set its next to the old head before changing head. This ordering preserves a reference to the existing sequence.
Move head to nine. The old nodes remain connected, so the logical list is now 9,1,2,3 without copying their values.
Begin the append traversal at nine. The current marker identifies a node reference, not a numeric array index.
Follow next from nine to one. The operation is constant work for this hop, but the number of hops depends on list length.
Follow next again to two. Three is still ahead, so this node is not the append endpoint.
Reach three, whose next is None. The loop condition now fails and identifies the place to attach a new node.
Set that next reference to node four. The final append update is local even though finding its location required a traversal.
Access zero-based index two by following two links from head nine, reaching node two. The code makes the locating cost explicit.
Use node one as predecessor and redirect its next to three. Node two leaves the live chain, while the successor sequence stays reachable.
Traverse from head to confirm 9,1,3,4. Head deletion and invalid positions need their own guards because they do not have the same predecessor arrangement.

lessons.title: Floyd cycle detection and safe loop removal
lessons.invariant: Fast advances twice as far; after detection, equal-speed pointers locate the entry.
lessons.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary pointers.
lessons.takeaway: Find entry, walk to its cycle predecessor, and cut the closing link.

steps.caption: Start both pointers at A
steps.why: Guard fast and fast.next before advancing two links.

steps.caption: Round 1: slow=B, fast=C
steps.why: Inside a cycle, the fast pointer gains one position per round and eventually meets slow.

steps.caption: Round 2: slow=C, fast=E
steps.why: Inside a cycle, the fast pointer gains one position per round and eventually meets slow.

steps.caption: Round 3: slow=D, fast=D
steps.why: Inside a cycle, the fast pointer gains one position per round and eventually meets slow.

steps.caption: Meeting proves a cycle; reset slow to head
steps.why: Keep fast at the meeting node, then advance both one link per step.

steps.caption: Walk together: slow=B, fast=E
steps.why: The equal-speed pointers meet at the cycle entry, including when the entry is the head.

steps.caption: Walk together: slow=C, fast=C
steps.why: The equal-speed pointers meet at the cycle entry, including when the entry is the head.

steps.caption: Find the cycle predecessor: D
steps.why: Starting at entry, stop at the node whose next returns to entry.
steps.code:
while tail.next is not entry:
    tail = tail.next

steps.caption: Find the cycle predecessor: E
steps.why: Starting at entry, stop at the node whose next returns to entry.
steps.code:
while tail.next is not entry:
    tail = tail.next

steps.caption: Cut E.next to remove only the closing edge
steps.why: All five nodes remain reachable once the back edge is removed.

steps.caption: Head-entry and self-loop cases use the same removal rule
steps.why: For A->A, entry and tail are A; cutting A.next makes a one-node acyclic list.
steps.code:
tail = entry
while tail.next is not entry: tail=tail.next
tail.next=None

check.question: How should a self-loop A.next=A be removed?
options: Skip detection because the list is small.
check.explanation: The entry and its cycle predecessor are both A. Cutting the closing next link preserves the node.

teaching.motivation: A corrupted next reference can make a linked traversal run forever; detection must distinguish a real cycle from ordinary repeated values.
teaching.background: Floyd detection uses node identity and two traversal speeds. Acyclic traversal eventually reaches None; inside a cycle, the faster pointer catches the slower one. Resetting one pointer to head and walking equally locates the entry, after which only the cycle closing edge needs removal.
teaching.objective: Detect a cycle, locate its entry and remove the closing link while preserving every node.
applications: A diagnostic tool can identify a circular next chain without allocating a set of all visited nodes.
A repair routine can restore a list that accidentally links its tail back into an earlier node.
teaching.summary: The pointers met at D, equal-speed walking found entry C, and the cycle predecessor E supplied the closing edge to cut. Finding entry first also handled a cycle beginning at head or a one-node self-loop.
teaching.next: This lesson reinforces pointer identity and reachability, which also matter in list reversal and graph traversal.
bridges: Use A->B->C->D->E with E returning to C. Both pointers begin at A, and the code guards fast and fast.next before a two-link advance.
After one round, slow reaches B while fast reaches C. The highlighted nodes show different distances traveled, not different stored values being compared.
After the next round, slow is C and fast is E. Neither has reached None, so traversal continues inside the reachable structure.
The third round puts both references at D. Meeting at the same node proves a cycle, even though D is not its entry.
Reset slow to head A but leave fast at the meeting D. The next phase changes both pointers to the same speed.
One equal-speed step gives B and E. The loop continues because they still identify different nodes.
The next step brings both to C, identifying the entry. This entry test also works when the entry is head.
Starting from entry C, advance a tail candidate to D. We are now looking for a node whose next returns to entry, not for another arbitrary meeting.
Advance to E and observe that E.next is C. This identifies the one closing link that makes the structure cyclic.
Set E.next to None. The entire A-through-E sequence remains reachable, but its final traversal now terminates.
For the self-loop A->A, entry and cycle predecessor are the same node. Cutting A.next applies the same removal rule without deleting the only node.

teaching.motivation: To report unusually warm days relative to the observed period, the threshold must come from the entire dataset rather than from each local prefix.
teaching.background: The arithmetic mean is total divided by count. This exercise naturally uses two passes: first compute the global mean, then count values strictly greater than it. A running sum and a running count each summarize processed data without storing a second copy.
teaching.objective: Derive a two-pass solution and distinguish above the mean from equal to the mean.
applications: A sensor summary can count readings exceeding the mean of a completed recording period.
A report can compare each daily workload to the overall observed average rather than an arbitrary fixed threshold.

Add ten to the running sum. The accumulator now summarizes exactly the first processed day.
Adding twenty brings the prefix sum to thirty. The highlighted cell marks new work while earlier values remain included in total.
Adding thirty gives sixty. No above-average decision has been made yet because the final total is not known.
Adding forty finishes at 100; dividing by four establishes mean 25. The threshold will stay fixed during the second pass.
Compare ten with 25 and leave count zero. The strict greater-than test matches the phrase above average.
Twenty also fails the comparison, so the count is still zero. Changing the threshold after each reading would solve a different problem.

lessons.title: Maximum fixed-width window sum
lessons.source: Slide 3; pages/cells 19 | Derived instructional solution; not an instructor-provided solution.
lessons.invariant: running is the current k-item sum; best is the maximum seen so far.
lessons.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
lessons.takeaway: Slide by subtracting the outgoing value and adding the incoming value.

steps.caption: Choose a valid fixed window width
steps.why: Require 1 <= k <= n; define or reject invalid inputs explicitly.
steps.code: if not 1 <= k <= len(a): raise ValueError()

steps.caption: Sum the first three values
steps.why: Build the first window in O(k), then reuse its sum.

steps.caption: Remove 2 and add 1
steps.why: Adjacent fixed-width windows share all but one outgoing and one incoming value.
steps.code:
running += a[right] - a[right-k]
best = max(best, running)

steps.caption: Remove 1 and add 3
steps.why: Adjacent fixed-width windows share all but one outgoing and one incoming value.
steps.code:
running += a[right] - a[right-k]
best = max(best, running)

steps.caption: Remove 5 and add 2
steps.why: Adjacent fixed-width windows share all but one outgoing and one incoming value.
steps.code:
running += a[right] - a[right-k]
best = max(best, running)

steps.caption: Return the maximum sum 9
steps.why: Tracking best separately keeps an earlier maximum even when the current window shrinks in sum.

check.question: Why does sliding avoid recomputing k values each time?
options: Neighboring windows differ by only two boundary values.
check.explanation: The shared interior sum is already included in running.

lessons.python:
def max_window(a,k):
    if not 1 <= k <= len(a):
        raise ValueError('Require 1 <= k <= len(a)')
    running = sum(a[:k])
    best = running
    for right in range(k,len(a)):
        running += a[right] - a[right-k]
        best = max(best,running)
    return best
a = [2,1,5,1,3,2]
assert max_window(a,3) == 9
print(max_window(a,3))

teaching.motivation: Computing every k-minute traffic total by summing k readings repeatedly wastes work because adjacent windows overlap almost completely.
teaching.background: A fixed-width window contains k consecutive values. Moving it one position removes one outgoing value and adds one incoming value. Maintain its sum and a separate maximum seen so far; this works with negative values as well, provided the initial maximum comes from a real window.
teaching.objective: Update a fixed-width sum in constant work per shift and retain the best window total.
applications: A traffic dashboard can find the busiest consecutive three-minute period in a completed record.
A signal-processing routine can maintain a rolling fixed-width aggregate without rescanning its whole buffer.
teaching.summary: The sums moved 8,7,9,6 by changing only the two boundary contributions. The maximum stayed nine even after the final current sum fell to six.
teaching.next: The same incremental-aggregate reasoning appears in rolling averages and more advanced window techniques.
bridges: Use [2,1,5,1,3,2] with width three. The validity check ensures there is at least one complete window and avoids an undefined initial result.
Sum the first window [2,1,5] to obtain eight. Initialize both running and best from that actual window.
Slide right by removing two and adding one, obtaining seven. The highlighted window overlaps the previous one in its two interior values.
Remove the outgoing one and add three, producing nine. best increases because this current sum exceeds every earlier window.
Remove five and add two, producing six. The current sum changes, but best remains nine, which is why two separate variables are needed.
Return nine for indices two through four, [5,1,3]. The final diagram revisits the best window rather than assuming the last window must win.

lessons.title: Stack ADT: last in, first out
lessons.source: Slide 4 pp1-5; 06-stack-and-queue cells3-16. Applications on p5 are uses, not separate worked algorithms.
lessons.invariant: Only the current top is available to peek or remove.
lessons.complexity: Linked-head/deque endpoint push/pop O(1); Python list append amortized O(1).
lessons.takeaway: The most recently pushed surviving item is removed next.

steps.caption: Start with an empty stack
steps.why: An empty stack has no valid top item; choose an explicit underflow policy.

steps.caption: Push A then B
steps.why: Both additions occur at the same exposed end.

steps.caption: Push C
steps.why: C becomes the top without changing A or B.

steps.caption: Peek without removal
steps.why: Peek returns the top value and preserves the stack state.

steps.caption: Pop returns C first
steps.why: Removal reverses the order of outstanding insertions.

check.question: After push(A), push(B), push(C), what does pop return?
check.explanation: LIFO returns the most recent unremoved item.

lessons.python:
stack = []
stack.append('A')
stack.append('B')
stack.append('C')
top = stack[-1]
assert top == 'C'
popped = stack.pop()
assert popped == 'C' and stack == ['A','B']
print(top, popped, stack)

teaching.motivation: Some tasks must resume the most recent unfinished action before an older one; unrestricted list access would allow the wrong removal order.
teaching.background: A stack exposes one end, called the top. push adds there, pop removes there, and peek reads without removal. This restriction creates last-in, first-out order. Empty-stack access requires an explicit policy, and operation cost still depends on the underlying storage.
teaching.objective: Predict push, peek and pop results from the current top.
applications: Undo history removes the newest recorded edit before older edits.
Nested function calls finish the newest active call before its suspended caller can resume.
teaching.summary: Pushing A,B,C made C the top; peek preserved it and pop removed it. LIFO describes that order, while linked-head, deque and array implementations determine the relevant cost guarantees.
teaching.next: Postfix evaluation and balanced-delimiter checking use a stack to remember the most recently unfinished subproblem.
bridges: Begin with no elements. The empty marker represents the absence of a top, so the code must not read or pop one yet.
Push A and then B at the same end. B is now the newest survivor and therefore the only removable item.
Push C above the existing items. The diagram orders the row from bottom to top, with the rightmost cell exposed.
Peek reads C through the top position without changing the sequence. Compare the unchanged boxes with the assigned top variable.
Pop removes C and reveals B. The resulting [A,B] makes the last-in, first-out rule concrete.

lessons.title: Queue ADT: first in, first out
lessons.source: Slide 4 pp6-9; 06-stack-and-queue cells17-31. Scheduling, spooling and BFS are application contexts.
lessons.invariant: Enqueue at the tail; dequeue the oldest surviving item at the head.
lessons.complexity: Deque or linked head/tail endpoints O(1); list.pop(0) O(n).
lessons.takeaway: FIFO describes order; the representation determines whether it is efficient.

steps.caption: Start with an empty queue
steps.why: The oldest and newest endpoints are absent until the first enqueue.

steps.caption: Enqueue A then B
steps.why: New items enter behind existing waiting items.

steps.caption: Enqueue C
steps.why: The oldest item is still A.

steps.caption: Dequeue A
steps.why: Removing from the front preserves the arrival order of B and C.

steps.caption: Avoid shifting an array-backed queue
steps.why: A Python list front deletion shifts its remaining elements; deque or head/tail links avoid that work.

check.question: Which endpoint receives a newly enqueued item?
check.explanation: Enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head implements FIFO.

lessons.python:
from collections import deque
queue = deque()
queue.append('A')
queue.append('B')
queue.append('C')
removed = queue.popleft()
assert removed == 'A' and list(queue) == ['B','C']
# Unlike deque.popleft, list.pop(0) shifts all remaining array slots.
slow_queue = ['A','B','C']
assert slow_queue.pop(0) == 'A'
print(removed, list(queue))

teaching.motivation: When requests should be served in arrival order, choosing the newest request first would violate the intended service policy.
teaching.background: A queue adds at its back or tail and removes at its front or head. This creates first-in, first-out order. A deque or linked head/tail representation supports local endpoint updates, while a plain Python list front deletion shifts remaining array items.
teaching.objective: Trace FIFO operations and choose storage that avoids linear front shifts.
applications: A basic printer spooler serves earlier submitted jobs before later jobs under a FIFO policy.
Breadth-first search processes earlier-discovered vertices first to advance one distance layer at a time.
teaching.summary: A,B,C entered at the tail and A left from the head, preserving waiting order. The final implementation comparison showed why an ordering contract does not by itself guarantee constant-time endpoint operations.
teaching.next: Round-robin scheduling adds unfinished work back to this queue instead of allowing one job to occupy every turn.
bridges: Start with an empty deque. No oldest or newest element exists yet, matching absent head and tail endpoints.
Append A and then B at the back. A remains at the front because it arrived first.
Append C behind B. The newest arrival changes the back endpoint but does not change which waiting item should leave next.
popleft removes A and leaves B,C in their original order. The next front is now B.
Compare that operation with list.pop(0), which would shift the array suffix. Both can return A, but deque storage supports the intended cheap front removal.

lessons.title: Stack and queue operations side by side
lessons.invariant: Stack exposes the newest survivor; queue exposes the oldest survivor.
lessons.complexity: Endpoint operations O(1) with appropriate linked/deque storage.
lessons.takeaway: The same inputs produce different removal orders because the ADT contracts differ.

steps.caption: Push and enqueue A
steps.why: The structures receive the same arrival sequence but expose different removal ends.

steps.caption: Push and enqueue B
steps.why: The structures receive the same arrival sequence but expose different removal ends.

steps.caption: Push and enqueue C
steps.why: The structures receive the same arrival sequence but expose different removal ends.

steps.caption: Stack removes C; queue removes A
steps.why: A stack reverses outstanding arrival order, while a queue preserves it.

steps.caption: Stack removes B; queue removes B
steps.why: A stack reverses outstanding arrival order, while a queue preserves it.

steps.caption: Stack removes A; queue removes C
steps.why: A stack reverses outstanding arrival order, while a queue preserves it.

steps.caption: Both structures are empty again
steps.why: A linked queue must clear tail when removing its last node. Guard removals from empty structures.
steps.code: if head is None: tail = None

check.question: Which removal sequence follows enqueues A,B,C?
check.explanation: FIFO preserves the arrival order.

lessons.python:
from collections import deque
stack, queue = [], deque()
for x in ['A','B','C']:
    stack.append(x)
    queue.append(x)
removed = []
for _ in range(3):
    sp = stack.pop()
    qp = queue.popleft()
    removed.append((sp,qp))
assert not stack and not queue
assert removed == [('C','A'),('B','B'),('A','C')]
print(removed)

teaching.motivation: Receiving the same values does not determine removal order; the ADT policy decides whether old or recent work comes next.
teaching.background: Stacks and queues are restricted sequence interfaces. Stack push/pop use one exposed end, giving LIFO; queue enqueue/dequeue use opposite ends, giving FIFO. Comparing them side by side isolates order from input data and from unrelated implementation details.
teaching.objective: Predict both removal sequences after identical arrivals and recognize the empty-endpoint case.
applications: An editor undo stack reverses the outstanding edit order, while a print queue preserves submission order.
A task planner chooses stack-like depth-first or queue-like breadth-first processing according to its exploration goal.
teaching.summary: The same arrivals A,B,C produced C,B,A from the stack and A,B,C from the queue. Both ended empty, when an implementation must restore its empty-state endpoint invariants.
teaching.next: Expression algorithms require stack order; scheduling and breadth-first traversal require queue order.
bridges: Insert A into both structures. With one item, newest and oldest coincide, so their behavior has not diverged yet.
Insert B and compare the two labels: stack top moves to B, while queue front remains A. The identical row contents now hide different exposed ends.
Insert C to complete the arrival sequence. The next removal depends on the ADT contract rather than on the stored values.
Pop the stack to obtain C and dequeue the queue to obtain A. These opposite answers reveal LIFO versus FIFO directly.
Both now return B, but for different reasons: it is the newest stack survivor and the oldest queue survivor.
The stack finally removes A while the queue removes C. Each structure has followed its own order consistently across all three removals.
Both are empty again. A linked queue would clear tail along with head here, preventing a stale endpoint on the next enqueue.

lessons.title: Infix, prefix and postfix notation
lessons.invariant: The expression tree meaning stays fixed while token order changes.
lessons.complexity: A well-formed postfix expression can be evaluated in O(n) tokens.
lessons.takeaway: Notation places operators differently; postfix makes evaluation order explicit.

steps.caption: Use the meaning a + b*c
steps.why: Multiplication binds before addition in conventional infix notation.

steps.caption: Expose the grouped subexpression
steps.why: Parentheses can make the implicit grouping explicit.

steps.caption: Put operators before operands
steps.why: Prefix writes the outer operation first, followed by its operand expressions.

steps.caption: Put operators after operands
steps.why: Postfix writes b and c before their multiplication, then applies addition.

steps.caption: Operand order still matters
steps.why: Subtraction and division are not commutative; a b - means a-b, not b-a.

check.question: What is postfix for a + b*c?
check.explanation: The product b*c is computed before adding a; the final + combines a with that product.

lessons.python:
a, b, c = 2, 3, 4
infix = a + b*c
grouped = a + (b*c)
prefix_tokens = ['+','a','*','b','c']
prefix_meaning = a + (b*c)
postfix_tokens = ['a','b','c','*','+']
postfix_meaning = a + (b*c)
assert infix == grouped == prefix_meaning == postfix_meaning
left, right = 8, 3
assert left-right == 5
print(infix, prefix_tokens, postfix_tokens, left-right)

teaching.motivation: A machine needs an unambiguous evaluation order even when a familiar written expression relies on human knowledge of precedence.
teaching.background: Operands supply values and operators combine them. Infix puts operators between operands, prefix puts them before operand expressions, and postfix puts them after. All three can represent the same expression tree; changing token order must preserve grouping and operand direction.
teaching.objective: Translate a grouped expression between infix, prefix and postfix without changing its meaning.
applications: A compiler can convert human-readable infix expressions into a form easier to evaluate mechanically.
A stack calculator can evaluate postfix tokens without consulting precedence rules during evaluation.
teaching.summary: The meaning a+(b*c) stayed fixed while notation moved its operators. The subtraction example emphasized that explicit order still matters even when precedence no longer needs to be inferred.
teaching.next: Operator precedence explains infix grouping; infix-to-postfix conversion and postfix evaluation implement the two processing stages.
bridges: Start with a+b*c, where multiplication binds more tightly than addition. The selected operator marks the subexpression that must be completed first.
Write the grouping explicitly as a+(b*c). This identifies the meaning that must survive every notation change.
Prefix places the outer + first, then a and the product expression * b c. The token order follows the expression structure rather than the original typography.
Postfix places b,c before *, then ends with + to combine their product with a. The final operator consumes complete operand expressions.
For 8 3 minus, the left operand is eight and the right is three. The result five shows why converting notation must not reverse operands.

lessons.title: Precedence and associativity, including exponentiation
lessons.invariant: Precedence chooses tighter grouping; associativity chooses grouping among equal-precedence operators.
lessons.complexity: Stack-based conversion processes each token a constant number of times overall.
lessons.takeaway: Exponentiation is right-associative; mathematical ^ is not Python exponentiation syntax.

steps.caption: Multiplication binds more tightly than addition
steps.why: Precedence groups 2+3*4 as 2+(3*4), giving 14 rather than 20.

steps.caption: Parentheses override the usual order
steps.why: An explicit group forces its interior result to be computed as one operand.

steps.caption: Equal-precedence multiplication and division group left
Exponentiation groups to the right
steps.why: In mathematical notation, 2^3^2 means 2^(3^2)=512, not (2^3)^2=64. Do not pop equal-precedence ^ for an incoming ^.

# exponentiation: right-associative
# pop higher precedence, not equal precedence

steps.caption: Translate the notation correctly in Python
steps.why: Python uses ** for powers; ^ is bitwise XOR. The slide table uses the mathematical power convention.

options: No; leave it until its right operand is completed.
Yes; all equal precedence is left-associative.
Only if it is written using Python XOR.
check.explanation: For a right-associative incoming operator, pop strictly higher precedence, not equal precedence. Python ** is exponentiation; ^ is XOR.

assert 2 + 3*4 == 14
assert (2+3)*4 == 20
assert 8/4*2 == 4
assert (8/4)*2 != 8/(4*2)
assert 2 ** 3 ** 2 == 2 ** (3 ** 2) == 512
assert (2 ** 3) ** 2 == 64
assert 2 ** 3 == 8
assert 2 ^ 3 == 1
print('Python ** is power; ^ is bitwise XOR.')

teaching.motivation: Two operators in one line can describe very different calculations depending on grouping, even when the tokens themselves stay unchanged.
teaching.background: Precedence decides which operator groups more tightly; associativity decides equal-precedence grouping. Parentheses override the defaults. Ordinary multiplication/division group left, while mathematical exponentiation groups right. Python writes exponentiation as **; its ^ operator instead means bitwise XOR.
teaching.objective: Determine expression grouping and apply the correct equal-precedence rule during conversion.
applications: A calculator parser needs right associativity to interpret chained powers correctly.
Porting mathematical pseudocode to Python requires replacing power notation rather than accidentally applying XOR.
teaching.summary: Precedence explained 2+3*4, parentheses deliberately changed it, and associativity resolved equal-priority operations. The Python examples separated mathematical meaning from the language spelling of its operators.
teaching.next: The operator-stack conversion lesson uses these grouping rules to decide when a pending operator can be emitted.
bridges: Compute 3*4 before adding two, producing fourteen. The diagram identifies tighter multiplication grouping, not simply whichever operator appears first.
Parentheses change that grouping to (2+3)*4, producing twenty. The changed answer shows why parentheses carry meaning rather than decoration.
For 8/4*2, equal precedence and left associativity group the division first. The code contrasts the resulting four with the different right-grouped expression.
For 2^3^2 in mathematical notation, the right-hand power completes first, giving 2^9=512. A converter must therefore leave an equal-priority pending power on the stack.
Python uses ** to express that power calculation. The final paired examples distinguish 2**3=8 from 2^3=1, preventing a notation error from masquerading as an algorithm error.

lessons.title: Why applications choose stacks or queues
lessons.source: Slide 4 pp5,8; conceptual application explanations. No backtracking or semaphore implementation is specified in these slides.
lessons.invariant: Choose the next task according to the intended newest-first or oldest-first policy.
lessons.complexity: Endpoint bookkeeping can be O(1); total application work depends on the tasks performed.
lessons.takeaway: The ADT order must match the application policy; a data structure alone does not guarantee fairness.

steps.caption: Backtracking remembers recent choices
steps.why: A stack can store choices or return points; the most recent unfinished branch is revisited first. This is a concept example, not another course algorithm implementation.

steps.caption: Undo the latest decision first
steps.why: Popping a failed decision returns to the previous branch point rather than the oldest one.

steps.caption: Function calls retain return points
steps.why: The most recent unfinished call returns before its caller can resume, matching LIFO.

steps.caption: Printer spooling can preserve arrival order
steps.why: A FIFO print queue serves job A before jobs B and C when that is the intended policy. Actual print systems may also support priorities.

steps.caption: Waiting policies need explicit guarantees
steps.why: A semaphore may use a waiting queue, but FIFO fairness is an implementation policy rather than a universal semaphore guarantee. Process scheduling and BFS also use queues under suitable policies.

check.question: Does choosing a semaphore automatically guarantee FIFO wakeup order?
options: No; its implementation and waiting policy determine fairness.
No; all semaphores are necessarily LIFO.
check.explanation: Queues are a possible mechanism for waiting tasks, but the synchronization API or implementation must specify the fairness policy.

lessons.python:
from collections import deque
choices = ['start','left']
choices.append('dead end')
failed = choices.pop()
assert failed == 'dead end'
def subtask():
    return 'subtask finishes before helper'
def helper():
    return subtask()
assert helper() == 'subtask finishes before helper'
print_queue = deque(['A','B','C'])
assert print_queue.popleft() == 'A'
# This is an explicit FIFO waiting-policy example, not a semaphore implementation.
waiting = deque(['task1','task2','task3'])
selected = waiting.popleft()
assert selected == 'task1'
print(choices, list(print_queue), selected)

teaching.motivation: A data structure is useful only when its removal policy matches what the application should do next.
teaching.background: LIFO suits nested unfinished work because the newest dependency must be resolved first. FIFO suits arrival-ordered service because earlier waiting work gets the next turn. These are policy choices: a queue can implement a fair waiting order, but synchronization primitives or service systems must actually specify that policy.
teaching.objective: Explain why an application fits stack or queue order without claiming guarantees its API never promises.
applications: Backtracking stores recent choices so a failed branch can undo its newest decision first.
A FIFO printer policy uses a queue to preserve submission order among waiting jobs.
teaching.summary: Backtracking and nested calls used newest-first order, while printer jobs illustrated oldest-first service. Semaphore waiting then showed the limit of the analogy: fairness depends on the chosen policy, not on the primitive name alone.
teaching.next: Concrete expression, scheduling and graph lessons turn these policy matches into complete procedures.
bridges: The choices start,left,dead end record a recent branch history. The rightmost failed choice is the next one that needs attention.
Pop dead end to return to the previous choice left. Removing the oldest start decision instead would skip the local branch context.
Nested calls follow the same dependency order: subtask finishes before helper can complete. The call-stack diagram represents suspended return points.
The printer example changes the desired order to A before B before C. Removing from the queue front matches this explicit FIFO service policy.
The waiting-task row is only an example of a FIFO policy. The code does not implement a semaphore or imply that every semaphore guarantees the same wake order.

options: Pop the stacked operator before pushing the new one.
check.explanation: Equal-precedence left-associative operations must be evaluated in the earlier-to-later order. Right-associative exponentiation needs a different equal-precedence rule.

teaching.motivation: Human-readable formulas rely on precedence and parentheses; a converter must preserve that meaning while producing tokens a stack evaluator can consume directly.
teaching.background: Infix-to-postfix conversion scans left to right. Operands can be emitted immediately, while an operator stack delays operations whose right operands are unfinished. Parentheses form boundaries; precedence and associativity decide when older operators can be completed before a new one is pushed.
teaching.objective: Trace output and operator-stack state and explain every push, pop and parenthesis removal.
applications: An expression parser can translate input formulas into postfix instructions for evaluation.
A formula editor can separate grouping analysis from later computation by storing a normalized operator order.
teaching.summary: The stack delayed *, protected the parenthesized group, emitted / before -, then completed the product before the outer addition. The final postfix order a b c / d minus * e + represented the original grouping.
teaching.next: Postfix evaluation consumes this completed order with a different stack that stores numeric values rather than pending operators.
bridges: Convert a*(b/c-d)+e. The three rows distinguish incoming tokens, completed postfix output and operators still waiting for their right-hand expressions.
Read a and emit it immediately. An operand already represents a complete value, so it needs no precedence decision.
Read * and push it rather than emit it. Its right operand has not been completed yet.
Read ( and place it above *. This boundary protects the outer product while the grouped expression is processed.
Read b and append it to output. The operator stack remains unchanged because no new operator has arrived.
Read / and push it above (. The slash must wait for its right operand c.
Read c and emit it. The output now contains both operands needed for the pending division.
Read minus, whose priority is below /. Pop / into output first, then keep minus waiting inside the group.
Read d and emit it. The group now has the right operand needed by its subtraction.
Read ) and emit operators back to (, producing the grouped postfix result b c / d minus. Remove the parenthesis itself because grouping symbols are not postfix instructions.
Read + outside the group. The completed product has higher precedence, so emit * before pushing the outer addition.
Read e and emit the final operand. The only unfinished operator is now the + waiting on the stack.
At end of input, flush that +. The output is complete and the empty operator stack confirms that no pending operation remains.

lessons.complexity: O(n) token processing; O(n) worst-case stack space.

check.explanation: The first pop is the right operand, and the second is the left operand.

teaching.motivation: Once an expression is in postfix order, evaluation can be driven by available values instead of re-reading precedence rules.
teaching.background: An operand stack holds completed subexpression values. A number is pushed; a binary operator pops its right operand first and its left operand second, computes left op right and pushes the result. A valid expression must never lack operands and must leave exactly one final value.
teaching.objective: Evaluate postfix expressions while preserving operand order and detecting invalid stack shape.
applications: A reverse-Polish calculator processes tokens using only a value stack.
A small expression interpreter can evaluate normalized formulas after infix parsing is complete.
teaching.summary: The tokens 8 2 / 3 minus produced four from the division and one from the subtraction. The final single stack value was the expression result, while operand shortages or leftover values would indicate invalid input.
teaching.next: Delimiter checking reuses stack order for structural validation rather than arithmetic values.
bridges: Evaluate 8 2 / 3 minus with a fresh empty stack. The token row is input; the other row will hold completed numeric results.
Push eight because a number is already a complete operand expression. No arithmetic is possible yet.
Push two above eight. The top value will become the right operand when an operator arrives.
For /, pop right=2 and then left=8, compute 8/2 and push four. Reversing these pops would change the result.
Push three above the completed result four. The stack now holds the two operands for the final subtraction.
For minus, pop three then four and compute 4-3=1. The operation replaces two operands with one completed value.
The stack contains exactly one value, so return one. The validation code rejects missing operands and surplus final values rather than treating them as valid expressions.

teaching.motivation: Matching the number of openers and closers is insufficient: a parser must also verify their types and nesting order.
teaching.background: Opening delimiters create unfinished groups. A stack records those groups so the most recent opener must be closed first. A closer is valid only when it matches the current top; finishing with leftover openers is also invalid. This lesson is a derived solution to the course exercise.
teaching.objective: Validate nested delimiter structure and explain failures caused by mismatches or unmatched ends.
applications: A source-code parser checks that brackets and parentheses form properly nested groups.
A structured-expression editor can warn when a newly typed closer does not match the innermost open group.
teaching.summary: The stack grew for open groups and shrank only for matching closers. The example ([]){} ended empty; the contrasting ([)] would fail at its first mismatched closer even with equal counts.
teaching.next: The same nested-state idea appears in function-call stacks and expression parsing.

Push (. The outer parenthesized group is now unfinished and stored as the current top.
Push [ above (. The square-bracket group must be completed before the outer parenthesis can close.
Read ] and match the top [. Popping that opener returns attention to the still-unfinished parenthesis.
Read ) and match (. The stack becomes empty because the first complete nested group has ended.
Read { and start a new independent group. An empty stack between groups does not by itself mean input processing is finished.
Read } and remove its matching {. No earlier group remains unfinished.
End of input now coincides with an empty stack, so accept. A leftover opener or an earlier wrong-type closer would have caused rejection.

teaching.motivation: To describe today price run, we need the distance back to the nearest earlier price that is strictly greater, without rescanning the same history repeatedly.
teaching.background: A stock span includes today and consecutive preceding days whose prices are no greater than today. A monotonic stack stores candidate boundary indices in decreasing-price order. When a new price dominates a candidate, that candidate cannot serve as a future nearest-greater boundary and can be removed permanently.
teaching.objective: Compute spans from previous-greater boundaries and explain the linear total work of stack updates.
applications: A price dashboard can report how many consecutive days a current price matches or exceeds.
The nearest-greater pattern also supports threshold-boundary calculations over ordered sensor histories.
teaching.summary: Each new price removed irrelevant lower-or-equal candidates and used the surviving nearest greater index as its boundary. Every day index entered once and left at most once, avoiding the repeated work of a naive backward scan.
teaching.next: Sunset visibility uses a related monotonic structure but a different equality rule because equal heights block.
bridges: Use prices [15,10,20,30,40,20,30,10,45,35]. The span counts today too, and the stack will hold indices rather than just prices so distances can be computed.
Day zero has no previous greater price, giving span one. Push index zero as the first possible boundary for later days.
Price ten is below fifteen, so index zero remains a greater boundary. The distance 1-0 gives span one.
Price twenty removes both ten and fifteen. With no greater price remaining, the span extends back through all three days.
Price thirty removes twenty and again leaves no boundary. The current day plus its three predecessors gives span four.
Price forty removes thirty and extends the span to five. The stack now needs only this newest record-high candidate.
Price twenty is blocked by the earlier forty, so the span restarts at one. Both indices remain useful because they represent decreasing candidate prices.
Price thirty removes the recent twenty but not forty. Its distance from the forty index is two.
Price ten is below thirty and finds that immediately preceding day as its boundary. The span is one despite the longer stack.
Price forty-five removes every candidate, so its span covers nine days. Those popped indices will never need to be reconsidered individually.
Price thirty-five is immediately bounded by forty-five and has span one. The output row now contains the complete result.
Compare with a naive backward scan that can revisit old days many times. The stack achieves linear total work because an index can be pushed once and popped at most once.

teaching.background: Buildings are ordered west to east, and sunset is to the west. A building is visible only when every earlier building is strictly shorter. A decreasing stack retains possible blockers; strictly shorter candidates can be popped, but equal-height candidates must remain.
