lessons.title: Round-robin scheduling with a ready queue
lessons.invariant: Every unfinished job has one queue entry and waits behind previously queued jobs.
lessons.complexity: O(K) queue operations for K time slices; O(J) space for J jobs.
lessons.takeaway: Run for a quantum; complete the job or put its remaining work at the back.

steps.caption: Give each job one time unit per turn
steps.why: Jobs are all available initially; unfinished jobs return to the queue tail.

steps.caption: Time 1: run A; requeue with 2
steps.why: Requeueing unfinished work behind all waiting jobs prevents one long job from occupying every turn.

steps.caption: Time 2: run B; complete
steps.why: Requeueing unfinished work behind all waiting jobs prevents one long job from occupying every turn.

steps.caption: Time 3: run C; requeue with 1
steps.why: Requeueing unfinished work behind all waiting jobs prevents one long job from occupying every turn.

steps.caption: Time 4: run A; requeue with 1
steps.why: Requeueing unfinished work behind all waiting jobs prevents one long job from occupying every turn.

steps.caption: Time 5: run C; complete
steps.why: Requeueing unfinished work behind all waiting jobs prevents one long job from occupying every turn.

steps.caption: Time 6: run A; complete
steps.why: Requeueing unfinished work behind all waiting jobs prevents one long job from occupying every turn.

check.question: Where does an unfinished job go after its quantum?
options: The back of the ready queue
check.explanation: Appending to the tail gives other waiting jobs their turns.

lessons.python:
from collections import deque
ready = deque([('A',3),('B',1),('C',2)])
quantum, time = 1, 0
completed = []
while ready:
    job, remaining = ready.popleft()
    used = min(quantum,remaining)
    remaining -= used
    time += used
    if remaining:
        ready.append((job,remaining))
    else:
        completed.append(job)
assert completed == ['B','C','A'] and time == 6
print(completed, time)

teaching.motivation: One long-running job should not prevent every shorter waiting job from getting a turn.
teaching.background: A round-robin scheduler stores ready jobs in a FIFO queue and gives each a fixed time quantum. It removes the next job, reduces its remaining work and either completes it or appends it at the back. This example assumes all jobs are ready initially and ignores context-switch overhead.
teaching.objective: Trace time slices, remaining work and queue order through job completion.
applications: An operating-system teaching model shares CPU turns among ready tasks.
A cooperative task processor can interleave incremental work so one large request does not occupy the entire service loop.
teaching.summary: With one-unit turns, B finished before C and A even though A arrived first. Requeueing preserved access to turns rather than completion order, and all six work units were eventually consumed.
teaching.next: Queue implementations determine endpoint cost; scheduling policy adds the rule for what happens after each removal.
bridges: Initialize A:3,B:1,C:2 and a quantum of one. Each label combines a job name with its remaining work, with the next job at the front.
Run A for one unit, leaving two. Because it is unfinished, append it behind B and C rather than running it immediately again.
Run B for its only unit and remove it permanently. A short job can now finish while a longer earlier job is still pending.
Run C for one unit, leaving one, then put it behind A. The queue tracks unfinished jobs only.
Run A again and leave one unit. Requeue it behind C so the waiting job still receives its turn.
Run C to completion. The completed row grows while only A remains ready.
Run the last unit of A and finish at time six. The completion order B,C,A reflects job lengths under repeated turns, not a violation of FIFO ready-queue service.

lessons.title: First non-repeating character in a stream
lessons.invariant: After front cleanup, the queue front is the earliest character seen exactly once.
lessons.complexity: O(n) total time; O(sigma) space for sigma distinct characters.
lessons.takeaway: Frequency answers uniqueness; a queue preserves first-appearance order.

steps.caption: Maintain counts and candidate arrival order
steps.why: Only the earliest candidate with count one can be the answer.

steps.caption: Read a; first unique is a
steps.why: Increment its frequency, enqueue only on first appearance, and remove repeated characters from the queue front.

steps.caption: Read a; first unique is #
steps.why: Increment its frequency, enqueue only on first appearance, and remove repeated characters from the queue front.

steps.caption: Read b; first unique is b
steps.why: Increment its frequency, enqueue only on first appearance, and remove repeated characters from the queue front.

steps.caption: Read c; first unique is b
steps.why: Increment its frequency, enqueue only on first appearance, and remove repeated characters from the queue front.

steps.caption: Read c; first unique is b
steps.why: Increment its frequency, enqueue only on first appearance, and remove repeated characters from the queue front.

steps.caption: Read b; first unique is #
steps.why: Increment its frequency, enqueue only on first appearance, and remove repeated characters from the queue front.

check.question: Why can a repeated character behind the front remain temporarily queued?
options: It is removed if it reaches the front; it cannot affect the current answer.
Its count becomes one again later.
The queue is sorted by frequency.
check.explanation: Lazy cleanup only needs the front to be valid. Counts never decrease in this problem.

teaching.motivation: A live stream changes which earlier characters remain unique; rescanning the entire prefix after every new character would repeat work.
teaching.background: Frequency counts tell whether a character has appeared once, while a queue preserves first-appearance order. Enqueue a character on its first occurrence, update its count on every occurrence and discard repeated characters from the front. A repeated character farther back can wait for lazy cleanup.
teaching.objective: Maintain the earliest unique character after every stream prefix using counts and a candidate queue.
applications: A streaming text monitor can display the earliest still-unrepeated symbol as input arrives.
The same first-seen queue plus counts can track the oldest uniquely occurring identifier in an append-only event stream.
teaching.summary: For aabccb, the answers were a,#,b,b,b,#. Counts detected repetition, and the queue made the earliest surviving candidate accessible without rescanning the prefix.
teaching.next: This combines two structures for complementary roles: a mapping answers frequency and a queue answers age order.
bridges: Process the stream aabccb one character at a time. The queue stores possible answers in first-seen order, while counts determine whether those candidates are still unique.
The first a gets count one and enters the queue. Its front position makes a the current answer.
The second a raises its count to two, so remove it from the front. With no candidate left, output #.
The first b enters the queue with count one. It is now the earliest unique character.
The first c enters behind b, but b remains the answer because it appeared earlier and is still unique.
The second c makes c repeated, but b still occupies a valid front. No need to remove c from the middle just to answer the current query.
The second b invalidates the front. Remove b, then the now-front repeated c, leaving an empty queue and answer #.

lessons.title: Reverse a singly linked list
lessons.invariant: prev heads the reversed prefix; curr heads the untouched suffix.
lessons.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
lessons.takeaway: Save next, reverse the link, then advance both pointers.

steps.caption: Reverse links without losing the unprocessed suffix
steps.why: Keep prev for the reversed prefix and curr for the next node to reverse.

steps.caption: Save A.next before overwriting it
steps.why: Without saved_next, reversing the link could lose access to the remaining nodes.

steps.caption: Reverse A.next
steps.why: The current node joins the reversed prefix; the saved suffix remains reachable.

steps.caption: Save B.next before overwriting it
steps.why: Without saved_next, reversing the link could lose access to the remaining nodes.

steps.caption: Reverse B.next
steps.why: The current node joins the reversed prefix; the saved suffix remains reachable.

steps.caption: Save C.next before overwriting it
steps.why: Without saved_next, reversing the link could lose access to the remaining nodes.

steps.caption: Reverse C.next
steps.why: The current node joins the reversed prefix; the saved suffix remains reachable.

steps.caption: Save D.next before overwriting it
steps.why: Without saved_next, reversing the link could lose access to the remaining nodes.

steps.caption: Reverse D.next
steps.why: The current node joins the reversed prefix; the saved suffix remains reachable.

steps.caption: Set head to the final prev node
steps.why: curr is None when the unprocessed suffix is empty. Empty and one-node lists work unchanged.

check.question: Why save curr.next before setting curr.next=prev?
check.explanation: The original next reference is the only path from curr to the rest of a singly linked suffix.

lessons.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, name, next_node=None):
        self.name, self.next = name, next_node
def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr is not None:
        saved_next = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev, curr = curr, saved_next
    return prev
head = Node('A',Node('B',Node('C',Node('D'))))
head = reverse(head)
values, current = [], head
while current is not None:
    values.append(current.name)
    current = current.next
assert values == ['D','C','B','A']
print(values)

teaching.motivation: Reversing a singly linked list should change its links without losing the only path to nodes not yet processed.
teaching.background: A singly linked node has no backward link to recover a lost suffix. Keep prev at the reversed prefix and curr at the untouched suffix, save curr.next before overwriting it, then redirect the link and advance. The result uses the original nodes rather than a copied value list.
teaching.objective: Reverse a chain in place while preserving the processed-prefix and unprocessed-suffix invariant.
applications: A linked data pipeline may need to invert traversal order without allocating another set of nodes.
Pointer-reversal reasoning is useful when implementing low-level sequence transformations and checking reachability.
teaching.summary: Each original next link was saved before becoming a backward link. Once curr reached None, prev identified D as the new head of D->C->B->A.
teaching.next: Doubly linked reversal adds a second field to swap; cycle detection provides another example of managing a few traversal references safely.
bridges: Reverse A->B->C->D with prev=None and curr=A. The two variables name a reversed prefix and an untouched suffix, initially empty and complete respectively.
Save A.next as B before any rewrite. Without that saved reference, disconnecting A could hide the rest of the chain.
Set A.next to None and advance prev to A, curr to B. A is now the complete reversed prefix.
Save B.next as C while it still points forward. The next step is allowed to change B only because C remains reachable through saved_next.
Redirect B.next to A, then advance to C. The reversed prefix has grown to B->A.
Save C.next as D before overwriting it. The invariant still separates completed reversed links from untouched forward links.
Redirect C.next to B and advance to D. The prefix now reaches C->B->A, and only D remains unprocessed.
Save D.next, which is None. That value will signal that the untouched suffix is exhausted after the final rewrite.
Redirect D.next to C and advance curr to None. Every node now belongs to the reversed prefix.
Set head to prev, which is D. The code returns the new head rather than leaving the old A endpoint as the entry to a one-node suffix.

lessons.title: Iterator and generator traversal
lessons.invariant: The iterator state identifies the next value to produce or signals exhaustion.
lessons.complexity: A simple traversal O(n) total; per-next cost depends on the iterator; generator storage depends on retained state.
lessons.takeaway: iter obtains traversal state; next advances it; yield suspends execution.

steps.caption: Create an iterator from an iterable
steps.why: The iterable provides an iteration protocol; the iterator holds traversal state.

steps.caption: next(it) returns 3
steps.why: The cursor advances after producing one value; earlier items are not automatically replayed.

steps.caption: next(it) returns 5
steps.why: The cursor advances after producing one value; earlier items are not automatically replayed.

steps.caption: next(it) returns 8
steps.why: The cursor advances after producing one value; earlier items are not automatically replayed.

steps.caption: Exhaustion raises StopIteration
steps.why: A for loop catches this signal to end traversal. A fresh iter(container) can start another pass.

steps.caption: A generator suspends at yield
steps.why: The next call resumes after the previous yield, retaining local state rather than storing every output.

steps.caption: Lazy generation trades storage for one-pass consumption
steps.why: The generator protocol is __iter__/__next__. Creating a generator does not run its full body or materialize all results.

check.question: What happens after a normal finite iterator is exhausted?
check.explanation: A for loop uses StopIteration as its normal end-of-iteration signal.

lessons.python:
values = [3,5,8]
it = iter(values)
assert next(it) == 3
assert next(it) == 5
assert next(it) == 8
try:
    next(it)
except StopIteration:
    exhausted = True
def numbers():
    yield 1
    yield 2
    yield 3
g = numbers()
assert next(g) == 1 and next(g) == 2
lazy = (2**x for x in range(10))
assert next(lazy) == 1
print(exhausted, list(g))

teaching.motivation: A for loop works over many container types because it asks for successive values through one protocol rather than assuming array indexing.
teaching.background: An iterable can provide an iterator; an iterator holds state for producing its next value. next advances that state or raises StopIteration. A generator is an iterator created from a function containing yield; it suspends and resumes execution instead of materializing its entire output immediately.
teaching.objective: Trace iterator exhaustion and generator suspension and explain the storage tradeoff of lazy production.
applications: A data reader can yield records one at a time rather than loading a full dataset.
A custom linked container can support for loops without exposing its internal next references to clients.
teaching.summary: The iterator returned 3,5,8 once and then signaled exhaustion. The generator demonstrated resumable execution, while lazy powers showed that saved execution state can replace a materialized output list.
teaching.next: Call-frame state helps explain generators, while ADT protocols show why distinct containers can support the same iteration interface.
bridges: Create an iterator over [3,5,8]. The container retains the data, while it stores the position of the next value to return.
The first next call returns three and advances the cursor. It does not remove three from the original container.
The next call returns five from the new cursor position. Traversal continues rather than restarting at the first element.
The third call returns eight and moves beyond the final available item. All values have now been produced once.
One more next call raises StopIteration. A for loop interprets that signal as normal completion instead of automatically rewinding the iterator.
The generator yields one, then two, pausing after each yield. Its retained local execution point explains how the next request can resume in the middle of a function.
The powers generator produces values only when requested. This saves materialized-output storage, but exhausted one-pass state cannot supply arbitrary repeated indexing like a stored list.

lessons.title: Recursion: base case, decomposition and composition
lessons.invariant: Every recursive branch decreases a well-founded size measure toward a base case.
lessons.complexity: For sum(n)=n+sum(n-1), time O(n) and CPython stack O(n).
lessons.takeaway: Solve a smaller version, stop at a directly answerable case, and combine the returned answers.

steps.caption: Define a smaller identical problem
steps.why: For sum(3), the smaller task is sum(2), not a different problem type.

steps.caption: Keep the pending composition
steps.why: The caller must add its own n after the smaller answer returns.

steps.caption: Continue to a base case
steps.why: A base case must have a direct answer without another recursive call.

steps.caption: Compose the answers upward
steps.why: Correctness follows when each smaller answer is correct and the composition preserves the intended meaning.

steps.caption: Check the domain and progress
steps.why: Calling sum(n) again with unchanged n would never reach the base case. Negative inputs need a documented policy.

rows.label: Valid input: each call moves toward zero
No progress: the same task keeps returning
Outside this function's domain: raise ValueError before recursion

check.question: A function has a base case but calls itself with unchanged n. Is termination guaranteed?
options: No; the calls may never reach the base case.
Yes; any base case guarantees termination.
check.explanation: Each recursive branch must make progress toward a reachable base case.

teaching.motivation: A problem can be easier to describe by solving a smaller version of itself, but that description is useful only if it stops and combines the smaller answers correctly.
teaching.background: Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller task. Decomposition chooses that smaller task; a base case is a task answered directly without another call; composition combines the returned smaller answer into the original answer. For sum 1 through 3, solve sum through 2, stop at sum through 0, then add the waiting numbers back.
teaching.objective: Identify the smaller task, direct-answer case and combining operation, and verify progress toward termination.
applications: A filesystem walk applies the same inspection procedure to each subfolder, stopping at files or empty folders.
A tree computation solves child subtrees and combines their results, such as summing their node counts.
teaching.summary: sum_to(3) became a smaller sum, reached the directly answerable zero case and returned through additions to six. Correct recursion required both a valid combination rule and a decreasing input that actually reached the allowed base case.
teaching.next: Call-stack frames explain how unfinished callers remember their additions; divide-and-conquer extends the idea to several smaller tasks.
bridges: To sum 1+2+3, ask for sum_to(2) rather than inventing a different kind of problem. That smaller same-shaped task is decomposition, and the highlighted recursive call expresses it.
The original caller still owes the addition of three after the smaller answer comes back. The pending 3+? row makes composition concrete: it describes work that has not happened yet.
Continue reducing the argument until sum_to(0), whose answer is directly zero. That is the base case, where the function can return without making another self-call.
Return zero, then add one, two and three in the waiting callers to obtain 0,1,3,6. The diagram shows how correct smaller answers become the larger answer rather than merely ending the recursion.

The three final rows test the design: 3->2->1->0 makes progress, repeated sum(3) never shrinks, and -1 lies outside the chosen domain and raises ValueError. A written base case cannot help a call sequence that never reaches it.

lessons.title: Call stack frames and unwinding
lessons.invariant: A suspended caller retains locals and its return point until its callee finishes.
lessons.complexity: A depth-d recursion retains O(d) frames unless the language/runtime optimizes it.
lessons.takeaway: Maximum live depth measures stack space; total calls measure work.

steps.caption: Call sum_to(3)
steps.why: The first frame stores n=3 and where to return.

steps.caption: Suspend the caller
steps.why: A new frame handles sum(2), while sum(3) waits.

steps.caption: Reach the base frame
steps.why: All pending callers remain live at the deepest point.

steps.caption: Unwind the stack
steps.why: The callee result replaces the pending call, then the caller returns its combined result.

steps.caption: Finish the original call
steps.why: Frames are released as calls return. A tree of many calls can have only linear simultaneous depth.

check.question: Which quantity controls recursion stack memory?
options: The number of distinct variable names
check.explanation: Each active or suspended call retains a frame until it returns.

lessons.python:
events = []
def sum_to(n, depth=1):
    events.append(('enter', n, depth))
    if n == 0:
        answer = 0
    else:
        answer = n + sum_to(n-1,depth+1)
    events.append(('return', n, answer))
    return answer
result = sum_to(3)
assert result == 6
assert max(e[2] for e in events if e[0]=='enter') == 4
print(events)

teaching.motivation: When a recursive caller pauses for a smaller answer, something must retain its local values and the point where execution should resume.
teaching.background: A call-stack frame records one unfinished function invocation, including arguments, local state and its return point. Calls push frames, and returns remove them. The maximum simultaneously live chain controls stack space; total calls measure a different resource, the overall work performed.
teaching.objective: Trace entry, suspension and return while distinguishing call depth from final output size.
applications: Nested directory processing retains each parent location until its child traversal finishes.
Debugging a recursive failure uses the stack trace to identify the chain of unfinished callers and their arguments.
teaching.summary: Four frames were live at the zero base case of sum_to(3). Unwinding replaced pending calls with results until the original frame returned six, demonstrating why a scalar answer can still require a linear-depth call stack.
teaching.next: Head/tail recursion changes where work is pending, while tree recursion separates the number of calls from the deepest live path.
bridges: Call sum_to(3) and create its first frame. It remembers n=3 and the fact that its caller expects a returned result.
The call to sum_to(2) adds a new frame while sum_to(3) waits. The earlier addition is unfinished, not forgotten.
Continue through sum_to(1) to sum_to(0). The four displayed live frames explain the maximum depth even though the base answer is just one number.
As calls return, replace each smaller call with its result and perform the waiting addition. The return values 0,1,3 show the order in which suspended work finishes.
The original frame adds three and returns six, then leaves the stack. The returned result no longer requires those unfinished-call records.

lessons.title: Head and tail recursion in Python
lessons.source: Slide 5 pp9-11; correction to the unqualified tail-recursion space claim.
lessons.invariant: A tail call has no pending computation after the recursive call returns.
lessons.complexity: Both head-style and tail-style depth-n recursion use O(n) CPython stack space.
lessons.takeaway: Tail position is a control-flow property; CPython does not eliminate tail-call frames.

steps.caption: Head-style processing waits for recursion
steps.why: The function first visits a smaller problem, then performs its own output step.
steps.code:
def head(n):
    if n == 0: return
    head(n-1)
    print(n)

steps.caption: Head-style work occurs while unwinding
steps.why: The deepest nonbase frame prints first.

steps.caption: Tail-style work happens before the final call
steps.why: An accumulator can carry completed work to the next frame.

steps.caption: The recursive call is the final operation
steps.why: There is no addition after tail_sum returns; return n+f(n-1) would not be a tail call.

steps.caption: Python still retains call frames
steps.why: The slide memory claim needs a runtime qualifier: tail-call optimization is not performed by CPython. Use a loop for constant call-stack space.

check.question: Is a tail-recursive Python sum automatically O(1) stack space?
options: No; CPython does not optimize away tail calls.
check.explanation: Tail position enables an optimization in some runtimes, but CPython keeps the frames.

teaching.motivation: Two recursive functions can make the same number of calls yet do their visible work at different points in the call-and-return sequence.
teaching.background: Head-style recursion performs its main work after the recursive call returns. A tail call is the final operation, with no pending computation after it; an accumulator can carry completed work forward. Some runtimes optimize tail calls, but CPython retains those frames, so a loop is needed to avoid that recursive stack growth.
teaching.objective: Recognize tail position and predict processing order without assuming Python tail-call optimization.
applications: A traversal that visits children before reporting a parent performs its parent work while returning.
An accumulator loop can replace a tail-recursive numeric computation when constant call-stack space matters.
teaching.summary: The head example produced ascending output during unwinding. The tail-sum example carried its result forward but still used recursive frames in Python; the loop version avoided those frames by updating one state repeatedly.
teaching.next: Tree recursion introduces multiple child calls, while explicit stacks show how pending tasks can be represented without recursive control flow.
bridges: head(3) first calls head(2), so it cannot append three yet. The displayed chain records the calls made before any output work occurs.
At the base, calls begin returning and append one, two, three in that order. The code position after head(n-1) explains the ascending result.
The tail-sum version updates an accumulator before its next call, moving through (3,0),(2,3),(1,5),(0,6). Completed work travels in the argument instead of waiting as additions.
The return of tail_sum(...) is the final operation. By contrast, return n+f(n-1) would still owe an addition after the recursive result.
CPython keeps the tail-call frames despite that final position. The loop performs the same accumulator updates without recursively growing a chain of calls.

lessons.title: Tree recursion, repeated subproblems and call counts
lessons.source: Slide 5 pp7,12-14; uses the recurrence rather than treating unequal branches as equal.
lessons.invariant: Each nonbase Fibonacci call expands into two smaller calls.
lessons.complexity: Naive Fibonacci O(2^n) time upper bound; O(n) maximum stack depth.
lessons.takeaway: A wide call tree can do exponential work while retaining only one root-to-leaf call path at a time.

steps.caption: Expand fib(4)
steps.why: A tree-recursive frame creates two recursive subproblems.

steps.caption: Expand its children
steps.why: The subproblem fib(2) already appears through more than one path.

steps.caption: Reveal repeated work
steps.why: Without memoization, equal arguments are recomputed rather than shared.

steps.caption: Separate total nodes from depth
steps.why: For n=4 there are 9 calls, but only 4 live frames on a deepest path.

steps.caption: Use the actual recurrence
steps.why: C(n) grows on the Fibonacci scale; O(2^n) is a valid upper bound, not the tight base of growth.

check.question: Why is naive Fibonacci expensive?
options: It stores the entire call tree simultaneously.
Its addition operation always takes exponential time.
check.explanation: Repeated calls create exponential total work; only a linear-depth path is live at once.

lessons.python:
def measured_fib(n, depth=1):
    if n < 2:
        return n, 1, depth
    left, left_calls, left_depth = measured_fib(n-1,depth+1)
    right, right_calls, right_depth = measured_fib(n-2,depth+1)
    return left+right, 1+left_calls+right_calls, max(left_depth,right_depth)
value, calls, depth = measured_fib(4)
assert (value,calls,depth) == (3,9,4)
counts = [measured_fib(n)[1] for n in range(6)]
assert counts == [1,1,3,5,9,15]
# C(n)=1+C(n-1)+C(n-2) is the actual call-count recurrence.
print(value,calls,depth,counts)

teaching.motivation: A short recursive formula can repeatedly solve the same small tasks, making total work grow far faster than the depth of the written problem.
teaching.background: Tree recursion makes multiple self-calls from one invocation. Naive Fibonacci asks for n-1 and n-2, so equal arguments appear on different branches and are recomputed. A depth-first execution keeps a root-to-leaf path live, not the entire conceptual call tree, separating exponential work from linear stack depth.
teaching.objective: Explain repeated subproblems and distinguish total call count from maximum live depth.
applications: Counting recursive calls helps detect a performance problem that small Fibonacci examples conceal.
Comparing repeated subproblems motivates later memoization, which reuses answers instead of recomputing them.
teaching.summary: fib(4) expanded into nine total calls but only four simultaneously live frames on its deepest path. The actual unequal-branch recurrence explained repeated work; O(2^n) was a valid upper bound, not an equality between the branches.
teaching.next: The Fibonacci task-stack lesson preserves this branching explicitly and shows why replacing calls alone does not remove repetition.
bridges: Expand fib(4) into fib(3)+fib(2). The two child tasks are smaller, but both require their own work before the parent can combine results.
Expand fib(3) next and observe another fib(2). An argument already present elsewhere in the tree is not automatically shared by ordinary function calls.
The repeated subproblem diagram exposes that duplicate work. Without a cache, separate appearances of fib(2) execute independently.
The code counts nine calls for n=4, while its depth measurement reaches four. These numbers describe total executed nodes versus the longest simultaneously live chain.
Write T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+O(1), preserving the unequal child sizes. This recurrence supports exponential growth without treating the two branches as identical.

lessons.title: Divide and combine: the merge-sort recurrence
lessons.invariant: Each level partitions the input into disjoint subproblems whose total size is n.
lessons.complexity: T(n)=2*T(n/2)+O(n), giving O(n log n) time; typical array merge uses O(n) extra storage.
lessons.takeaway: Two half-sized calls plus linear combining creates linear work per level over logarithmically many levels.

steps.caption: Start with eight items
steps.why: Merge sort decomposes by position before it combines by value.

steps.caption: Split into two half-sized problems
steps.why: There are two calls of size four; their sizes sum to eight.

steps.caption: Split again
steps.why: Four calls of size two still total eight input positions.

steps.caption: Reach one-item base cases
steps.why: There are log2(8)=3 split levels before unit-size subproblems.

steps.caption: Combine sorted halves
steps.why: Merging scans each participating item a constant number of times per level. The full algorithm lesson covers detailed comparisons.

check.question: Why is total merge work O(n) at one level?
options: Disjoint subproblem sizes at that level sum to n.
There is only one subproblem at every level.
check.explanation: Each input position participates in one subproblem per level, and combining is linear in the subproblem size.

teaching.motivation: Dividing a problem in half is not enough to determine runtime; the cost of combining the half-sized answers matters too.
teaching.background: Merge sort divides an array by position, recursively sorts its two halves and merges the sorted results. At any one level, disjoint subproblem sizes sum to n, so linear combining work per subproblem totals O(n). Halving reaches unit-size bases after O(log n) levels.
teaching.objective: Explain the recurrence 2*T(n/2)+O(n) using subproblem sizes and work per level.
applications: Sorting large records can use repeated divide-and-combine stages instead of checking every pair.
Recurrence analysis helps compare algorithms with the same two recursive calls but different combining work.
teaching.summary: The eight-item example split into 4+4, then four twos and eight ones. Each level still accounted for eight positions; linear merging across logarithmically many levels gave O(n log n) total work.
teaching.next: The detailed merge-sort lesson follows the actual comparisons that combine two sorted halves.
bridges: Begin with [8,3,6,1,7,2,5,4]. The recursive code first divides positions; it does not need the input to be sorted before splitting.
Two child problems each have size four. Their sizes total eight, which is why the recurrence has two half-size calls.
Each four splits into two twos, producing four subproblems. Although the number of tasks grows, their combined input length remains eight.
Eight one-item pieces are direct sorted bases. Three halving levels were enough because log2(8)=3.
Returning calls merge already sorted halves into [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]. Each level processes a linear total of items, connecting the state diagram to the n log n bound.

lessons.title: Iteration, recursion and explicit stacks
lessons.invariant: Equivalent versions must preserve the same pending work and result.
lessons.complexity: A loop can avoid recursive frames; an explicit stack still stores pending tasks.
lessons.takeaway: Changing control flow alone does not automatically reduce the number of subproblems.

steps.caption: Specify a repeated computation
steps.why: An iterative accumulator can represent work already completed.

steps.caption: Move completed work into the accumulator
steps.why: One loop state replaces a chain of pending sum calls.

steps.caption: Finish the loop
steps.why: The result is the same as recursive sum_to(3).

steps.caption: Use an explicit work stack for branching
steps.why: A Fibonacci task can expand into n-1 and n-2 tasks; their base contributions are accumulated.

steps.caption: Representation changes, repeated work remains
steps.why: The notebook explicit-stack Fibonacci still expands the same exponential family of subproblems.
steps.code: # memoization would be a separate algorithmic change

check.question: Does replacing recursive Fibonacci with the notebook explicit task stack make it linear time?
check.explanation: Both versions expand the same subproblems. Memoization or bottom-up dynamic programming would change that work.

teaching.motivation: Changing a recursive function into a loop can reduce call-frame overhead, but it does not automatically change how much algorithmic work is required.
teaching.background: Iteration stores progress in loop variables. Recursion stores pending work in call frames, and an explicit stack can represent that work manually. Equivalent versions must preserve both completed results and unfinished tasks; reducing repeated subproblems requires an additional algorithmic change such as caching.
teaching.objective: Compare accumulator loops, recursive calls and explicit task stacks without confusing representation changes with work reduction.
applications: A loop can compute a sequential sum without retaining n recursive callers.
An explicit traversal stack can make pending branches inspectable while preserving recursive exploration behavior.
teaching.summary: The sum loop kept only current n and total. The Fibonacci task stack replaced recursive control with explicit pending arguments but still expanded the same repeated subproblems, so it did not become linear-time merely by using while.
teaching.next: The sum and Fibonacci lessons trace those two examples in full; call-stack analysis explains their storage differences.
bridges: Start sum-to-three with n=3 and total=0. The loop state stores completed work directly rather than leaving an addition pending in another frame.
Add three and decrease n to two. These two updates encode both the accumulated result and the smaller amount of work remaining.
Continue to n=0 and total=6, then return. The loop has reused one small state instead of keeping a chain of suspended sum calls.
For Fibonacci, one current counter is insufficient because a task branches into two tasks. The explicit stack stores those unfinished arguments.
Expanding tasks still creates duplicate Fibonacci subproblems. The highlighted extend operation changes where work is recorded, while the number of expansions remains exponential.

lessons.title: Iterative and recursive summation
lessons.invariant: Each recursive call returns the sum 1+...+n for its own n.
lessons.complexity: O(n) time; iterative O(1) space; recursive O(n) CPython stack.
lessons.takeaway: A recursive caller remembers unfinished addition; an iterative accumulator stores completed work.

check.question: What extra space does recursive sum_to(n) use in CPython?
options: O(1), because the result is one number
check.explanation: The depth-n chain keeps suspended callers alive.

teaching.motivation: Sequential summation is simple enough to compare completed-work accumulation with pending-work recursion using exactly the same mathematical goal.
teaching.background: To sum integers 1 through n, an iterative loop adds each value to a running total. A recursive version asks for the sum through n-1 and adds n after that result returns, stopping at zero. The lesson distinguishes this inclusive definition from sum(range(n)), which excludes n.
teaching.objective: Trace both forms, state their endpoints and explain their different auxiliary-space costs.
applications: A recursive sum is a compact model for reasoning about decreasing arguments and returned-answer composition.
An iterative aggregation is preferable when a long input should not consume one Python frame per element.
teaching.summary: The loop accumulated 1,3,6,10 as work completed. The recursive calls delayed additions until sum_to(0) returned, then reached the same ten; range(4) instead summed only 0 through 3.
teaching.next: Factorial reuses the same call structure with multiplication and a different identity base value.
bridges: Compute the inclusive sum 1+2+3+4. The first loop update adds one, establishing the initial processed-prefix total.
Add two to the previous one, giving three. The accumulator already contains completed work, so no caller needs to wait for this addition.
Add three to obtain six. The highlighted prefix now includes the first three positive integers.
Add four to obtain ten and finish the loop. This gives the result against which the recursive version can be checked.
Now request sum_to(4), which cannot finish until sum_to(3) returns. The call-stack row replaces the accumulator view with pending additions.
sum_to(3) requests sum_to(2), keeping its own three available for later. Smaller calls do not erase the suspended caller state.
sum_to(2) requests sum_to(1). Each argument decreases by one, so the sequence is progressing toward zero.
sum_to(1) requests sum_to(0). The last positive addition is still waiting rather than having occurred already.
sum_to(0) returns the direct base answer zero. This is the turning point from making calls to completing callers.
Unwind by adding one, two, three and four to obtain ten. The final comparison with sum(range(4))=6 prevents confusing inclusive and excluded endpoints.

lessons.title: Recursive factorial and pending multiplication
lessons.invariant: factorial(n) returns n! for a nonnegative integer n.
lessons.complexity: O(n) multiplications; O(n) CPython stack; big-integer arithmetic adds bit costs.
lessons.takeaway: The base value is 1; unwind by multiplying each saved n.

steps.caption: Enter factorial(4)
steps.why: Wait for factorial(n-1), then multiply by n.
steps.code:
if n <= 1: return 1
return n * factorial(n-1)

steps.caption: Enter factorial(3)
steps.why: Wait for factorial(n-1), then multiply by n.
steps.code:

return n * factorial(n-1)

steps.why: Wait for factorial(n-1), then multiply by n.
steps.code:
if n <= 1: return 1
return n * factorial(n-1)

steps.caption: Enter factorial(1)
steps.why: The base case returns 1.
steps.code:
if n <= 1: return 1
return n * factorial(n-1)

steps.caption: Return factorial(2) = 2
steps.why: Each returning frame performs exactly one pending multiplication.

steps.caption: Return factorial(3) = 6
steps.why: Each returning frame performs exactly one pending multiplication.

steps.caption: Return factorial(4) = 24
steps.why: Each returning frame performs exactly one pending multiplication.

steps.caption: State the domain and arithmetic model
steps.why: Require a nonnegative integer. Counting multiplications as constant work is a simplification because factorial values grow in bit length.

check.question: Why is factorial(0)=1 useful in the recurrence?
options: It is the multiplicative identity needed for 1*factorial(0).
check.explanation: The product of no factors is 1, giving a consistent base for n! = n*(n-1)!.

teaching.motivation: Factorial provides a small example in which every recursive caller has a multiplication waiting for the smaller result.
teaching.background: For a nonnegative integer n, n! is the product 1 through n, with 0!=1 as the empty-product identity. The recurrence n!=n*(n-1)! decreases n and combines by multiplication. Counting multiplications as constant work is a simplified model because the integers become larger as n grows.
teaching.objective: Trace factorial calls and returns and explain why the base value must be one.
applications: Counting arrangements of distinct items uses factorial values in elementary combinatorial models.
The example teaches pending multiplication and recursive composition before more complex tree algorithms.
teaching.summary: The calls decreased from four to one, then multiplied returned results into two, six and twenty-four. Nonnegative input validation and the multiplicative identity completed the definition, while Python retained the recursive frames.
teaching.next: Hanoi and tree recursion add multiple child tasks; iterative factorial can avoid the call-depth storage cost.
bridges: Request factorial(4). The function must obtain factorial(3) before its multiplication by four can finish.
factorial(3) similarly waits for factorial(2). The stack grows because earlier multiplications are still pending.
factorial(2) requests factorial(1), decreasing the argument again. This chain will reach a direct base rather than branch.
factorial(1) returns one. The base result preserves multiplication instead of annihilating every caller result as zero would.
The waiting factorial(2) multiplies 2*1 and returns two. The first pending composition has now completed.
factorial(3) multiplies 3*2 and returns six. Its child frame is finished before this caller returns.
factorial(4) multiplies 4*6 to produce twenty-four. The original requested result has now been reconstructed.
The last state records 0!=1 and the nonnegative domain. The code rejects negative inputs, and its operation count must be qualified if large-integer multiplication costs matter.

check.question: What is fib(4) with fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1?
check.explanation: The sequence is 0,1,1,2,3 for indices 0 through 4.

teaching.motivation: An explicit stack can reproduce a recursive branching computation, making its unfinished tasks visible without making the repeated work disappear.
teaching.background: Fibonacci uses fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1 and fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2). The notebook stack version expands each larger integer task into two smaller tasks and accumulates base contributions. Because the stack is LIFO and children are appended n-1 then n-2, the n-2 task runs next.
teaching.objective: Trace an explicit work stack and show why it computes Fibonacci without memoizing repeated arguments.
applications: A work stack helps inspect what a recursive procedure would still need to execute.
Comparing this expansion with caching demonstrates why storing results, not merely replacing recursive syntax, removes repeated subproblems.
teaching.summary: The stack expanded fib(4), encountered three fib(1) leaves and accumulated three. Repeated fib(2) tasks were still executed separately, preserving exponential total work despite replacing implicit calls.
teaching.next: Tree-recursion analysis explains its cost, and later dynamic-programming methods can reuse those repeated answers.
bridges: Start with the single task fib(4) and result zero. The stack represents work still owed; the accumulator contains only completed base contributions.
Expand four into tasks three and two. Two is on top because it was appended last, which determines the next displayed state.
Expand the top two into one and zero. This creates two base tasks while the earlier three remains waiting.
Process zero and add nothing. Removing a zero task still completes work even though the numeric accumulator does not change.
Process one and increase the accumulator to one. The pending three task now becomes exposed.
Expand three into two and one. This creates another fib(2), showing explicitly that the earlier computation was not cached.
Process the new top one and raise the total to two. The remaining two still needs expansion.
Expand that two into one and zero. The same small task pattern has appeared again through another branch.
Process zero and keep the total at two. There is now only one remaining base contribution.
Process the last one to reach three, leaving no pending tasks. An empty stack means all branches have contributed.
Return three and compare with the sequence 0,1,1,2,3. The agreement establishes the result while the repeated task expansion explains why the implementation remains expensive for large n.

lessons.title: Tower of Hanoi: the recursive move plan
lessons.invariant: Each rod is ordered largest at bottom to smallest at top.
lessons.complexity: Exactly 2^n-1 moves; O(2^n) time; O(n) recursion depth.
lessons.takeaway: Move n-1 aside, move the largest disk, then move n-1 onto it.

steps.caption: Move three disks from A to C
steps.why: Only top disks move, and a larger disk may never be placed on a smaller one.

steps.caption: Move 1: disk 1, A -> C
steps.why: The recursive plan first clears the n-1 smaller disks, then moves the largest, then brings the smaller disks onto it.
steps.code:
hanoi(n-1, src, aux, dst)
move_top(src, dst)
hanoi(n-1, aux, dst, src)

steps.caption: Move 2: disk 2, A -> B
steps.why: The recursive plan first clears the n-1 smaller disks, then moves the largest, then brings the smaller disks onto it.

steps.code:

steps.code:
